stories.headline: After offseason chaos, the Red Wings have an 'us against the world' mentality
stories.summary: A captain's trade request, a key young player's holdout and a resigned general manager. Here's how the Red Wings are holding it all together.
stories.body:
All the Detroit Red Wings wanted was puck drop on a new season.

It was the only way.

The only way to -- finally -- turn the page on a tumultuous offseason of gossipy headlines that deposited Detroit under an unwelcome (and unrelenting) spotlight. There was captain Dylan Larkin's trade request in June, Steve Yzerman abruptly stepping down as general manager in July, key restricted free agent Simon Edvinsson remaining unsigned and no new front office leader in place until the announcement of interim general manager Shawn Horcoff just two days before training camp opened in late September.

The Red Wings -- fresh off missing the playoffs for a tenth straight year in 2025-26 -- limped their way into another preseason anyway. Larkin, stripped of the team's captaincy, was there but soon injured. Edvinsson, still without a contract, came to town as well (before going home to Sweden on the heels of his own trade request). It felt as though the drama was reaching a fever pitch faster than Detroit could get to that first real game, where the team's play -- and not some media machine -- could do the talking.

Promise. Hope. Belief. The Red Wings had it all just hours away from their first real outing. The slate would be clean, the energy refreshed.

"It's us against the rest of the world," defenseman Moritz Seider said. "That's something we've learned pretty fast; with how much noise there is around this team. I think there are plenty of reasons to be anxious or nervous. But it's like, even if we didn't know who the [full-time] GM was at the start of camp, like, what changes? Nothing, really, because he's not the one who's setting the standard, who's setting the tone on the ice, and he's definitely not going to go out there and help us to win games.

"We have everything in place to be a good hockey team, and it just comes down to each and every one of us to be the best version of ourselves. We have really come together as a group and feel we were just more excited than anything."

Seider and his teammates echoed similar allegiances of brotherhood and held tightly to them heading into player introductions before Game 1 of 84 was underway. But the assembled crowd at Little Caesars Arena didn't bring its rose-colored glasses (a plain-clothed Larkin receiving resounding boos during his pregame recognition? Foreshadowing!) because even before the team's coming display, the franchise's faithful was already despondent.

Because not getting a deal done with Edvinsson and having Larkin's situation unresolved weren't their only grievances with Detroit's front office. The Red Wings' season began with Alex DeBrincat as a key pending unrestricted free agent in July, and the club had whiffed on a mid-September deadline to get DeBrincat locked in on a maximum eight-year extension before the league's new collective bargaining agreement makes seven years the longest a player can agree on. Management also didn't retain fan favorite veterans such as Patrick Kane -- who walked back to Chicago in free agency -- and then to have Larkin lingering and now even available to play, it could suddenly feel like death by a thousand cuts for the franchise.

There was some good news coming. Detroit signed DeBrincat to a seven-year, $91 million deal Wednesday to help cushion the blow of its now 1-3-2 record -- but even that couldn't fully quell concerns over the Red Wings' tenuous prospects for the season.

Then Detroit actually began to play. And the knife poked in a little deeper. The Red Wings were bad -- so bad that midway through the 2-0 shutout loss to New York in their home opener, choruses of "sell the team" echoed (on multiple occasions) from inside a building (established in 2017) that still hasn't hosted an NHL postseason game. And Detroit hadn't even fallen to Rangers' star goaltender Igor Shesterkin. Backup Dylan Garand shut the door.

Game 2 of the year was another home loss (3-2 to Winnipeg). Detroit was 0-2 to start a season for the first time since 2015-16 (and then, at least, they'd been on the road). An injury to Marco Kasper (since placed on injured reserve with an upper-body injury) against the Jets loomed large. The Red Wings were fine at 5-on-5 but terrifically awful on special teams.

Basically, it was going to be a long year in Detroit. Or so it seemed. But the Red Wings had miles to go before being truly counted out. Larkin would be back for their third game of the season. The kinship -- which had been a rallying cry for players repeatedly in the past -- was still intact. All Detroit needed was to ignore the mounting sense of crisis, clean up its early incompetence, win a few games and get on track toward what was supposed to be the year when it turned everything around against all odds.

It was now or never all too soon for Detroit to put actions behind words. That remains -- like the Red Wings -- a work in progress as Detroit languishes already in the Atlantic basement with a 1-3-1 record. There will be no reprieve then for a group that has been taking it on the chin from detractors for months. The Red Wings have to show that true change is not only still possible but also probable.

That has meant being realistic about what they are and aren't while uncovering an evolving identity. Whatever Detroit intends to become must be forged from less-than-ideal circumstances. The time, as ever, was nigh.

"I think we've done a pretty good job keeping the noise out of here," DeBrincat said. "I think we know what we can do. Maybe we deserve better in these games, a couple more bounces can go our way. But we have to work for it. It's not just going to come to us. We're not skilled enough to expect to go out there and score six goals. We have to be more crisp and bring that mentality a little bit higher. We'll be good. We're in the right spots, we're just not executing on the plays and we're not putting it in the net. We have plenty of chances to win these games."

From his lips, to the hockey gods' ears.

DETROIT NEEDED A VICTORY. In more ways than one.

During NHL draft weekend in June, it was a shocking development when news leaked that Larkin had asked for a trade from the club that drafted him 15th overall in 2014. The team's top center, who has amassed 645 points in 811 career games with 30-plus goals in each of his last five seasons, has five years remaining on his eight-year, $69.6 million contract that includes a no-trade clause.

Larkin originally said he wanted to land only in Vegas, Florida or Minnesota. However, he reportedly widened the net to include Dallas, Washington, Colorado and Tampa Bay, leaving Yzerman (and now Horcoff) with scant leverage to gain an adequate return on the team's star player. And so, Larkin remains a Red Wing -- albeit one without a letter -- and, as such, one of their best forwards. Having Larkin healthy after he suffered an upper-body injury working out in the gym was best for Detroit's prospects on the ice.

Larkin was cleared to return for Detroit before the Red Wings faced Ottawa. He didn't miss a beat, scoring a goal in the first period and adding an assist on Viktor Arvidsson's power-play strike in the second period to help Detroit earn its 5-3 win that delivered a much-needed shot in the arm after its frustrating start.

It meant something to have Larkin involved in a positive turn of events for the team. Granted, the cloud hanging over his unfulfilled ask isn't going to miraculously dissipate. But until it comes to fruition (or not), the Red Wings don't want to fracture internally. Larkin acknowledged during the preseason that, "I asked for a trade from the Detroit Red Wings as a captain and that has consequences" and expressed that, through his actions, he wanted to "build trust with my teammates again and with the fans."

That is why he went out with the others during those poorly received player introductions before the season opener. Larkin had to expect his presence would spark some displeasure. But he went out there anyway. Coach Todd McLellan could sympathize with the heat Larkin took, knowing too it wasn't entirely undeserved or unexpected.

"Dylan, today, being a part of the team, he wanted to be out there for the ceremony," McLellan said after Detroit's first loss. "Dylan's explanation was, 'I don't want the rest of my teammates, the ones that aren't dressed, to not be out there,' so, we went out as a team. Obviously, he's got to live with the ramifications of asking for a trade. It's not comfortable for anybody. I feel bad for him, I do."

Winning, though, is a salve. It has the power to reduce some friction. There is no doubt Detroit's lineup is strongest with Larkin in it, and his interactions with teammates (who have carefully toed the line with their own comments on his whole mess) remain characteristically jocular.

It was a pleasant realization for McLellan that by the end of training camp, the Red Wings' room wasn't badly splintered after what had been said -- and not done -- all summer. Those individual bonds forged through the years seemingly remained -- and were perhaps tight enough to also see Detroit past some early-season adversity.

"With everything that's going on around our organization -- and there's been a lot -- just the unity of the players right now is fairly good," McLellan said ahead of the Red Wings' final preseason game. "I had some concern about that. Not that they were going to be torn apart, but just how they were going to deal with all of this stuff, and to this point, in the locker room, the practices, the intermingling that I do with the group, they're handling it fairly well, and I don't want to say that's a surprise, but that's good to see and hear. But we'll still have some rough water ahead of us, and we're going to have to deal with things."

McLellan spoke with the weariness of a coach who has been there -- in the darkest depths of a freefall -- with his team. Maybe he is still a little haunted. Maybe he will be again.

Detroit's bench boss saw his team squander its promise just last season, starting the campaign quite opposite this one. The Red Wings stormed off then with nine wins in their first 13 games and were primed to snap out of their playoff doldrums. When the league halted on Feb. 6 for its Olympic break, the Red Wings sat third in the Atlantic and seventh in the NHL with 72 points. But Detroit returned to the ice three weeks later and dropped straight off a cliff, cratering defensively and sputtering offensively, so that the woeful 8-12-4 record it produced through the final 24 games (good for 28th overall in that stretch) left it once again on the outside looking in.

It was another lost season. Another missed opportunity. And the failure naturally played a part in Larkin -- now 30 years old and with only five postseason appearances to his credit from a long-ago rookie campaign -- antsy to move out of the Motor City. If Larkin was possibly feeling revitalized along with his teammates to secure that first victory of the season and put up a united front of sorts against the proverbial onslaught, the sentiment wouldn't last long.

Detroit dropped its next game (a fourth straight home outing) to Seattle 6-3. Then the Red Wings finally got on the road to Montreal in their first back-to-back of the year, but found their luck unchanged in a 1-0 shootout loss.

The Red Wings had plummeted to the Atlantic basement, sitting 29th in offense (averaging two goals per game) despite taking the third-most shots on net (32.8), and with a woeful 26th-ranked penalty kill (70%).

If that weren't bad enough, Larkin was courting discord in La Belle Province as well. The game hadn't even started when fans serenaded their visitors with refrains of "we want Larkin" in a cheeky attempt to work the Canadiens onto Larkin's third draft of a trade list.

This time, when asked about the Larkin circus, McLellan wasn't taking the bait.

"I'm sick and tired of talking about it," McLellan said after the game. "I'm not talking about it anymore, so I apologize."

Larkin did his best to diffuse the situation but with a hodgepodge of comments that seemed to both welcome and reject the Bell Centre's special attention.

"It was interesting," Larkin said. "I never would have imagined that in this building and in my career. But they are passionate fans. In my opinion, it's the best atmosphere in hockey. They're knowledgeable and love their team. That's how I read into it...[but] I don't have any control over that tonight. I give the guys in here a lot of credit, we played hard tonight."

Pressed further on whether he would want to play in Montreal, Larkin signaled his fidelity back to the Red Wings.

"I'm not going to go there," he said about considering other locales. "Because I'm on this team."

IT WILL STAY that way until it doesn't. The problem for Detroit is that while McLellan did praise the Red Wings' "internal group" for "shielding each other and getting ready to play," it was impossible to deny that Larkin's ongoing presence wasn't doing some damage five games into the season with a 1-3-1 record.

"I'd be lying if I said everything going on wasn't a distraction," McLellan said. "But we have a responsibility to each other to focus on what we can control and that's what we do."

There is that glaring piece of the puzzle -- the not winning bit -- that is a collective shortcoming, though. So it has to be a joint effort now too, in the present, not to let another year of potential upswing slip through their fingers too fast. There is only so much Detroit's players can manage themselves, anyway. On-ice performance is one thing. But to McLellan's point, so is cultivating the proper attitude in how they view the narrative and react to it.

Seider's mission is to be on the right side of setting a positive tone in that respect.

"I want to be the guy who is coming to the rink with a good mood," he said. "I want to be making sure even our oldest or youngest guys feel comfortable, making sure everyone is in a good spot, everyone is heard. And then also still holding each other accountable to the highest standard possible. That's something I really want to look forward to. Be dialed in at practice, be good in the gym, and just lead by example. And if I can do that, I think I do my part to drive this team forward."

Yzerman took some heat before abdicating his post as general manager for not doing more to bolster the Red Wings in free agency -- Arvidsson was the team's only major signee on a two-year, $10 million pact -- but there might be a silver lining to avoiding turnover. Arvidsson is decidedly low-maintenance, and Detroit has otherwise been able to focus on its entrenched core and rising stars, including Emmitt Finnie and rookie defenseman Anton Johansson.

The latter was an unanticipated addition to the roster -- the only perk to Edvinsson's mismanagement leaving a lineup spot open -- who pushed his way onto the scene and right next to Justin Faulk on Detroit's second pairing. Detroit drafted Johansson 105th overall in 2022. McLellan had called Johansson the "surprise" of Detroit's preseason play, and Johansson made the most of his NHL debut against New York carrying the third-most minutes among Detroit's defenders (with 19:10).

Johansson and Edvinsson aside, the Red Wings are running it back. That has made it easier on Detroit's incumbents to navigate the surrounding uncertainty because it's being done with actual friends. They've shared tough times together before; there is comfort in facing unfamiliarity as a unit now, too.

"It's really noticeable that guys were glued together this year; you could see it early on in training camp," Lucas Raymond said. "Guys were going hard. It was competitive. And I feel like that's the way you get tighter as a team. A lot of us have been in this for a long time with each other, which helps. The couple new guys that have come in have fit right in with our team too, both on and off the ice. So, it's still good vibes."

And don't let it be said that Detroit has completely lost its edge. During its tilt with the Senators, it was Finnie, the talented forward coming off a 30-point rookie season and gamely transitioning from the wing to center, who recorded his first NHL fight with Ottawa defender Jordan Spence in the second period. Unfortunately, the fisticuffs took place while a few other battles were happening, and Finnie didn't get a penalty or official acknowledgement of his milestone. Still, it will be recorded on his personal fight card for posterity and reflected the mindset Finnie had about how to approach this season of unease.

"It's really just about knowing that, every day, you're going to war with some of your brothers," Finnie said. "It definitely makes an impact. It makes the energy stay high and good. This group feels very close, and that goes a long way for us in here."

And it is possible that having already weathered their share of storms has taught the Red Wings some lessons to apply now in staying even-keeled about their current state. It just remains to be seen if Detroit's up-and-down opening to the NHL's extended slate was reflective of the upheaval having an effect, or if it was just a negative response to a shorter runway into the year from which Detroit is still capable of taking flight.

"It's going about our business, more than anything," DeBrincat said. "I think every year you try to block out the noise anyways, however it comes, and bond as a group early in training camp, and I feel like we did a good job of that so far. We've ignored a lot. We know what we can do. We have to stay confident, right? It's important for us to come together and stick up for each other in every way possible."

THE RED WINGS ARE SAYING all the right things. About the camaraderie and the connection and apparently unshakeable union that exists within the four walls of their room.

It has all been repeated before, too, when Detroit was sliding its way down the standings. The Red Wings' lack of results in a results-based business has been consistent with their pledges of ongoing fellowship.

So what changes now? Setting aside the past and those decisions outside player jurisdiction, how will the Red Wings take themselves to the vaunted -- if clichéd -- "next level" where we bear witness to the postseason contender they believe lurks beneath the surface of critical commentary?

Well, how does one eat an elephant? With a single bite at a time.

"I think we just have to take it day by day," Seider said. "Honestly, as silly as it sounds, but there's such a great stretch here in the first few weeks, where we are at home a lot, where you can really grind out some big wins and hopefully get going in the right way. I think that this will be a great challenge for us, to not look too far ahead but just take it game by game and try to maximize on our advantages as much as we can."

It is hard to say anything is out of reach after only a handful of games into an NHL campaign. The palpable sense of renewal coming off the Red Wings going into their season hasn't entirely worn off yet. DeBrincat was on to something. Detroit has to accept what it is and is not in order to do what Seider said, and it must capitalize on the things it can do well. Even if it is still figuring some of that out. Seider is also calling for accountability, and that's what Detroit has the power to accept now as well.

Evolution is inevitable, if only the Red Wings can lean into it.

"Obviously everyone knows there's a lot of things that's been going on with this team and around this team," Raymond said. "But I think for us when we came in here, it was nice, when it was just the guys, coaches, everyone around our team, and you kind of just locked it down and started focusing on hockey. Which is what we all want to do. Guys have been excited. And I've got a good feeling about this year."

stories.headline: 2027 NFL draft Big Board rankings: Mel Kiper's top 25 prospects, best by position
stories.summary: Seven quarterbacks ranked in the top 25? This NFL draft class could be fun. Mel Kiper Jr. stacks the best players on the board as we hit the midway mark of the college season.
stories.body:
I'm already getting excited for the 2027 NFL draft. This class could be really, really good. We have elite wide receivers, standout defenders and a bunch of excellent quarterback prospects. I've been holding off on ranking the best players available until we had a big enough sample of tape, but with roughly half the 2026 college football season in the bank, I'm ready to debut my Big Board for 2027.

My normal disclaimer: This is not a mock draft. What follows isn't any form of prediction for when or where players will get picked once we hit Round 1 on April 29 in Washington D.C. Instead, this is simply my personal ranking of the best players in the class. The list below is based on my own evaluations from what I see on film and some conversations I've had around the NFL. And remember that a lot can change here. Players will rise and fall on the board, and some will even return to school for another year at the collegiate level before turning pro in the future.

Here is my current ranking of the top 25 prospects in the 2027 draft class, which includes a ton of QBs. And at the bottom, I've included the best players at each position. Check back regularly right through draft day -- I will keep this list updated as the class continues to take shape. But one spot that might not change at all is No. 1 ...

Jump to:

Positional rankings

1. Jeremiah Smith, WR, Ohio State
Height: 6-foot-4 | Weight: 222 pounds

2026 stats over six games: 48 catches, 916 receiving yards, 11 touchdown catches

Smith is very clearly the best player in this draft class. He's big, fast and physical, and he snatches the ball on the run cleanly. On 281 career targets, he has just six drops. And Smith has the body control to make tough catches. I love the way that he is always looking to improve, too. Smith worked on his after-the-catch skills heading into the 2026 season, and he has been able to make some things happen with the ball in his hands using his strength and speed.

Ohio State continues to feed him targets (north of 10 per game), and nobody can cover him. That was very apparent against Illinois in September, when he caught 12 balls for 217 yards and four touchdowns. In three seasons at Ohio State, he has 38 career touchdown catches, and he's averaging 16.5 yards per catch. Just an incredible football player.

2. Drew Mestemaker, QB, Oklahoma State
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 215

2026 stats over five games: 67.5% completion rate, 1,575 passing yards, 13 touchdown passes, five interceptions; 136 rushing yards, two rushing touchdowns

Mestemaker didn't even start at quarterback for his high school team; he was the punter, played some safety and was the backup QB. Then he walked on at North Texas in 2024 as a QB before becoming the starter in 2025. After throwing for more than 4,000 yards, Mestemaker transferred with coach Eric Morris to Oklahoma State. It's an incredible story.

His toolbox is also pretty incredible. I love the way he scans the field and bides his time in the pocket. Mestemaker has the big arm to make all of the throws, with 30 completions going for 20-plus yards this season (third in the FBS). But he also has the mobility to pick up nice chunks of yardage on the ground. Mestemaker shows linebacker-esque toughness and plays with a competitive edge. He doesn't turn 21 years old until January, and he has just 20 career starts to his name. So, there's a lot of untapped potential.

3. Leonard Moore, CB, Notre Dame
Height: 6-2 | Weight: 197

2026 stats over five games: Eight tackles, four pass breakups

Moore is exactly what NFL coaches look for in a lockdown cornerback. He has elite length and ball skills, with seven interceptions and 22 pass breakups over his three-year career. He's scheme versatile, too. Moore displays great awareness and instincts in coverage, and he's a silky smooth mover. His footwork is truly outstanding. Moore consistently performs at a high level, but he's still looking for his first pick of the season. He missed the Oct. 10 game against Stanford because of a concussion.

4. Darian Mensah, QB, Miami (Fla.)
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 205

2026 stats over five games: 84.2% completion rate, 1,438 passing yards, 15 touchdown passes, zero interceptions; 97 rushing yards, two rushing touchdowns

Mensah is at his third program in three years, transferring from Tulane to Duke (where he had 34 touchdown passes last season) and then on to Miami. To date, he has started 32 college games -- great experience for a kid who doesn't even turn 22 until January. He is a smooth, fluid passer with solid accuracy. He's smart in the pocket and manages the game really well. And the mobility is there for him to beat a defense as a rusher when the situation calls for it.

Mensah currently leads the nation in completion percentage (84.2%) and QBR (92.5), and he's third in yards per attempt (10.8). Scouts are getting excited for Miami's trip to South Bend in November to play Notre Dame -- that game is going to say a lot about Mensah's draft stock because the Hurricanes have played a pretty light schedule thus far.

5. Colin Simmons, Edge, Texas
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 246

2026 stats over five games: 17 tackles, 9.5 sacks, 12 tackles for loss, 20 pressures, two forced fumbles, three run stops

Did you catch Simmons against Tennessee in September? He had 5.5 sacks in that game alone. The production is off the charts -- he has 30.5 sacks, 40.5 tackles for loss and eight forced fumbles over three seasons. And in 2026, he is leading the nation in sacks (9.5), tackles for loss (12) and pressure rate (23.0%). Simmons is the type of closer most NFL defenses want rushing off the edge.

Simmons is explosive out of the blocks with natural bend, and he can beat opponents with outside or inside moves. And he isn't given enough credit for the power element in his game.

6. Trinidad Chambliss, QB, Ole Miss
Height: 6-0 | Weight: 205

2026 stats over five games: 70.1% completion rate, 1,435 passing yards, 11 touchdown passes, four interceptions; 147 rushing yards, five rushing touchdowns

A lot will be made about Chambliss' smaller frame and the fact that he'll be 25 years old before the 2027 NFL season even begins, but he's the ultimate point guard at the quarterback position. I'm really impressed with his pocket presence and mobility, and the mechanics are sound. Chambliss puts zip on his passes with a nice tight spiral and avoids turnovers (seven career picks). And he's a playmaker who sees the field well, often relying on his legs to pick up first downs -- or score. Chambliss has 13 rushing TDs over the past two seasons.

Since transferring in from Fresno State and taking over for Austin Simmons early last season, Chambliss has played his best on the brightest stages. He always seems to respond when he's challenged. He's a real leader on offense.

7. Chris Cole, LB, Georgia
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 235

2026 stats over six games: 30 tackles, 2.5 sacks, 7.5 tackles for loss, 10 pressures, seven run stops, three pass breakups

Cole is all over the field every Saturday. He's 235 pounds but looks like a safety at the second level. Cole is quick to diagnose thanks to his football IQ and then flies to the ball, especially in lateral pursuit. He is going to be a combine standout with that tremendous speed.

He is versatile, too. Cole can line up off the ball on the inside or on the outside, and he will consistently make plays against the run, in coverage and as an occasional pass rusher -- I see solid bend and burst off the edge. Cole is an outstanding player and is perfect for the way NFL football is played today.

8. CJ Carr, QB, Notre Dame
Height: 6-2 | Weight: 215

2026 stats over six games: 70.8% completion rate, 1,378 passing yards, 16 touchdown passes, one interception; 78 rushing yards, three rushing touchdowns

There's a lot to like in Carr's game. He's smart and processes quickly before and after the snap, which is part of the reason he has taken just two sacks all season. He's accurate to all levels and throws with anticipation. And while his arm strength is good but not great, he can cause conflict for defenses with his mobility. Carr can throw on the move or pick up a first down on the ground. Nothing phases him, and he's always in control. In short, Carr is pretty advanced in the key areas of NFL-level quarterback play.

Just as it is for Darian Mensah on the other sideline, the Nov. 7 matchup with Miami will be important -- but the looming BYU matchup should also show us what Carr can do against strong competition.

9. Dylan Stewart, Edge, South Carolina
Height: 6-5 | Weight: 250

2026 stats over three games: Five tackles, 1.0 sacks, 2.0 tackles for loss, 10 pressures, two forced fumbles, one run stop

Stewart hasn't played much in the early part of the season. He missed the opener as he recovered from a back injury, and then he was suspended for one game for punching an Alabama player in the helmet and arguing with coaches on the sideline. But when he is playing, you can tell pretty quickly. His traits jump off the tape. It's just a matter of whether the production can catch up; Stewart has 12 career sacks over three seasons despite recording 78 pressures over those 27 games.

Stewart can vary his path to the QB, and he closes quickly with speed to power. He also has the big frame to hold the point and shed blockers against the run. The pass-rush ability is there, but he needs to figure out how to translate his physical traits into stat-sheet production on a more consistent basis.

10. Austin Simmons, QB, Missouri
Height: 6-4 | Weight: 220

2026 stats over six games: 64.8% completion rate, 1,434 passing yards, 14 touchdown passes, one interception; 50 rushing yards

This might be a little bit of a surprise to some folks, but go watch the tape. There is no better thrower of the football in the collegiate ranks right now than this young lefty -- he's a pure passer. Simmons can sling it with the best of them -- the ball explodes out of his hands. But he's also very accurate and mixes in good touch with all that velocity. Simmons transferred from Ole Miss after a 2025 season in which he was hurt early and lost his job to Trinidad Chambliss, and his electric arm has allowed Missouri to hit big plays down the field in 2026. Simmons is 12th in the nation with 10.6 air yards per attempt.

What's holding him back? Simmons has started just eight career games. His experience is still going to be pretty light by the end of the season, and that might scare some NFL teams. There's a chance Simmons returns to school for another year, but he deserves to be here on the Big Board because of his outstanding skill set and high ceiling.

11. Charlie Becker, WR, Indiana
Height: 6-4 | Weight: 208

2026 stats over six games: 30 catches, 529 receiving yards, eight touchdown catches

I love the way Becker attacks the football. He consistently wins in tight coverage with his big frame, excellent hands and nice adjustments to find the ball in the air. Becker can locate the open spots in the coverage, and he can stretch the field with his speed. He has averaged 17.6 yards per reception this season. I'll be watching him at the combine; he is going to test really well and should post a pretty fast 40-yard dash time.

12. Cam Coleman, WR, Texas
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 204

2026 stats over five games: 17 catches, 318 receiving yards, five touchdown catches

The traits are there. Coleman displays outstanding body control and the catch radius to haul in throws outside the strike zone. He's very good in contested catch situations, and he has brought in a few deep balls this season, helping his per-catch average up to 18.7. After two seasons at Auburn, Coleman came to Texas with a lot of hype. But the Longhorns' pass game has been a little uneven, and Coleman has seen only 27 targets through five games.

13. Ashton Hampton, CB, Clemson
Height: 6-2 | Weight: 205

2026 stats over five games: 15 tackles, one interception, nine pass breakups, 0.5 tackles for loss

Hampton's confidence shows in his play. You can tell he loves matching up with the opposition's No. 1 receiver and going to battle. And more often than not, Hampton wins. He has allowed just 2.5 yards per pass attempt in his direction this season, which ranks in the top 20 in the nation.

He plays an aggressive style, crowding receivers at the line of scrimmage, getting in his hip pocket and disrupting routes right away. Hampton can plant and drive on the ball (though his ball production is only moderate, with four career picks), and he has the recovery speed to make plays with his back to the QB when necessary.

14. Jadan Baugh, RB, Florida
Height: 6-1 | Weight: 225

2026 stats over six games: 110 carries, 672 rushing yards, 12 rushing touchdowns; seven catches, 46 receiving yards

Baugh is tied for the FBS lead in rushing touchdowns (12), and he's tied for ninth in rushing yards per game (112.0). He has it all, including really good field vision, breakaway speed and shiftiness. Baugh can cut back to make defenders miss, and he has the power to break tackles. He's a handful to bring down, and he almost never puts the football on the ground -- he hasn't fumbled since 2024, and that was his only career fumble across 1,000-plus offensive snaps. Baugh is also dependable as a receiver out of the backfield when called upon.

15. Greg Johnson, G/C, Minnesota
Height: 6-6 | Weight: 325

2026 stats over six games: Six starts, zero sacks allowed, one pressure allowed

Johnson has played significant snaps at left guard and center this season, and he's a high-level blocker at both spots. Versatility is one of his best traits; he had 50-plus snaps at both tackle spots last season in addition to his work on the interior. Johnson is a strong run blocker, with an aggressive, nasty edge to his game. He's powerful and can sustain well. But he also anchors well in pass protection, and he has never allowed a sack across 43 career games (34 starts).

16. Will Echoles, DT, Ole Miss
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 315

2026 stats over five games: 13 tackles, 0.5 sacks, 3.0 tackles for loss, nine pressures, six run stops, one pass breakup

NFL teams love penetrating, disruptive interior defensive linemen, and Echoles gets into opponents' backfields on a consistent basis. He had 11.5 tackles for loss and five sacks in 2025, and while the sacks haven't really come yet in 2026, he's causing headaches for QBs with nine pressures. Echoles is explosive and can beat double-teams with his high effort level. He's also very effective in lateral pursuit. And I like his professional approach to the game.

17. Jordan Seaton, OT, LSU
Height: 6-5 | Weight: 307

2026 stats over six games: Six starts, zero sacks allowed, zero pressures allowed

Seaton has started 28 games at left tackle, including 22 at Colorado before transferring to LSU before the 2026 season. And he has not allowed a sack since 2024. He can push blockers past the QB and has improved as a run blocker, showing the ability to pull there. Seaton is in great shape this season, and he looks the part. He just needs to be coached up a little to realize his full potential as an elite left tackle.

18. Yhonzae Pierre, Edge, Alabama
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 251

2026 stats over six games: 17 tackles, 2.5 sacks, 3.5 tackles for loss, 15 pressures, one forced fumble, two run stops, one interception, two pass breakups

As his eight sacks and 40 pressures of 2025 suggest, Pierre is a good pass rusher. But what I really like about his tape is the way he seals the edge and takes care of the run. He made 10 run stops last season. He does a nice job changing direction. Pierre is a complete player who will get after the QB, stop ball carriers in their tracks and drop into coverage against the pass. Check out his pick-six from early September against East Carolina.

19. Kade Pieper, G, Iowa
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 298

2026 stats over six games: Six starts, zero sacks allowed, two pressures allowed

Pieper has played primarily right guard, but he's versatile, and some scouts might see him as a center in the pros. He's an athletic blocker who can pull and get to the second level to help spring big runs. He's also effective driving defenders off the ball. Over 32 career games (19 starts), Pieper has not allowed any sacks.

20. Kelley Jones, CB, Mississippi State
Height: 6-4 | Weight: 205

2026 stats over five games: 17 tackles, six pass breakups, 1.5 tackles for loss

I had an eye on Jones last season for the 2026 class before he went back to school, and his consistency over these past two seasons is impressive. He anticipates well in coverage, and he uses his huge 6-foot-4 frame and long arms to attack receivers in press and make plays on the ball. Jones has only two interceptions (both last season), but he has broken up 17 passes since the start of 2025.

Jones can fly, too. He could put up a really good 40 time at the combine in March. He's comfortable with his back to the QB and is disruptive at the catch point. And he's a willing tackler in run defense.

21. Trevor Goosby, OT, Texas
Height: 6-7 | Weight: 325

2026 stats over five games: Five starts, zero sacks allowed, zero pressures allowed

Goosby is technically sound with the ability to drop an anchor in pass protection and the powerful hands to move defensive ends off the ball in the run game. As a run blocker, his strength and ability to carry out combo blocks stand out. He has solid length to handle pass rushers, and he has allowed just two sacks over 35 career games (20 starts). Most of that experience has been at left tackle, and Goosby projects there in the pros. "Consistent" is the one word I'd use to describe his game, and he maximizes his ability.

22. Ellis Robinson IV, CB, Georgia
Height: 6-0 | Weight: 180

2026 stats over six games: 13 tackles, one interception, four pass breakups

Physical kid. He isn't afraid to step up and make a tackle. He gets a little grabby in coverage at times, but he won't get pushed around by receivers. The playmaking spiked last season, too, when he picked off four passes in his first season as a starter. Robinson has one INT so far in 2026, but he has also broken up four passes on 19 balls thrown his way. He shows the speed to handle vertical routes, and he seems to be getting more and more consistent in coverage.

23. Trevor Lauck, OT, Iowa
Height: 6-5 | Weight: 314

2026 stats over six games: Six starts, zero sacks allowed, three pressures allowed

Yet another Iowa offensive lineman makes the list. Lauck has been a mainstay at left tackle since the beginning of last season, starting 19 games there over that time (one sack allowed in 2025, none this season). His pass protection traits have stood out in particular this season, as he's technically sound. I see good footwork and balance on the tape, and he sustains well and finishes his blocks.

24. Arch Manning, QB, Texas
Height: 6-4 | Weight: 222

2026 stats over five games: 63.0% completion rate, 1,122 passing yards, 10 touchdown passes, five interceptions; 174 rushing yards

Manning has dropped to QB6 on my board -- but he's still a top-25 player because of the skill set. I see the size, mobility and arm strength that NFL teams look for in a franchise quarterback. He can make throws rolling out, and he is dangerous as a runner (10 rushing touchdowns last season).

But Manning is too inconsistent, especially when it comes to accuracy and decision-making. He's going to be a tough evaluation. Watch just about any game he plays, and you'll ride the roller coaster of getting excited about his NFL ceiling and then wondering whether he's ever going to truly put it all together. Manning doesn't see the field as well as other quarterbacks on this list, and he occasionally throws off balance. And while the accuracy is better this season than it was in 2025, it still has to improve. I'm very curious to see how the rest of this season plays out.

25. Dante Moore, QB, Oregon
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 220

2026 stats over four games: 69.7% completion rate, 926 passing yards, nine touchdown passes, zero interceptions; 22 rushing yards

Moore hasn't played since September, when he took a hit against USC and suffered a concussion. He's back at practice, but he has already been ruled out for Saturday's matchup with Nebraska.

When Moore is at the top of his game, he's an impressive passer. He changes arm angles, he's mechanically sound, he displays precise ball placement, and there's good touch on his deep ball. Throws look effortless because of his arm strength, and he can deliver strikes while rolling out. There's even some scramble ability there. The toolbox is full.

But he has to show he can take over some games against top-tier competition. His performance against Penn State in 2025 (at a time when the Nittany Lions were the No. 3 team in the country) was exceptional. I thought he was going to build on that and enter the 2026 draft as one of the top QBs on the board. But he couldn't bottle that performance and repeat it against other top teams over the rest of that season. He now has a chance to prove he can rise to the matchup this year -- most notably against Ohio State on Nov. 7.
