stories.headline: Dembélé jokes he might ask for more holidays after PSG's win at Man City
stories.summary: Ousmane Dembélé joked he might ask coach Luis Enrique for more time off after starring in PSG's 4-2 win at Manchester City in the Champions League.
stories.body:
Ousmane Dembélé joked he might ask coach Luis Enrique for more time off after starring in Paris Saint-Germain's 4-2 win at Manchester City in the Champions League.

The Ballon d'Or winner scored one goal and assisted on another in Wednesday's game. Luis Enrique had rested him after the recent international break, allowing Dembélé to sit out Saturday's home game against Le Mans, and he looked razor-sharp against City.

"After the international break I went on holiday. Actually, I might ask for more holidays," Dembélé told broadcaster Canal Plus. "I really enjoy playing on Tuesday and Wednesday, especially when I come back from holiday. It's a real pleasure."

Asked if he would go on holiday again, a smiling Dembélé added: "It's possible, until March I think. It's the coach who decides."

PSG have a trip to Strasbourg in Ligue 1 on Saturday, ahead of another high-profile Champions League game at home to Lamine Yamal's free-scoring Barcelona next Tuesday.

Luis Enrique may again rest players. He also omitted left-back Nuno Mendes against Le Mans, while Dembélé sat out a game against Lille in Ligue 1 earlier this season.

Dembélé won the French league's best player award last season, despite starting only nine games in PSG's title-winning campaign. The decision to award him the trophy over other players who played significantly more games led to criticism.

City coach Enzo Maresca said PSG enjoy a luxury his team and other Premier League sides don't have, being able to rotate players against modest Ligue 1 sides.

"They can manage players when they play games before the Champions League," he said. "For us, it's a bit different, especially when you go [to] Anfield."

City played Premier League rival Liverpool in a heated atmosphere on Sunday, giving Maresca's side one day less to prepare for the PSG game.

Last season, the French league accepted PSG's request to postpone their game against title rival Lens to allow better preparation for a Champions League quarterfinal against Liverpool -- a decision perceived by some observers as preferential treatment.

PSG went on to win the trophy for a second straight year, beating Arsenal on penalties in the final.

Dembélé has scored three Champions League goals, but has not yet found the net in four Ligue 1 matches this season. PSG are in sixth place after six rounds and some performances have fallen below expectations.

"We couldn't care less that people doubted us. We're in October, it's only the second game of the Champions League," he said. "We just need to stay on track during the first half of the season and prepare for the second."

However, he acknowledged PSG's concentration dropped off against City.

"We eased up a bit in the second half," Dembélé said. "When you do that against players like that, you pay for it."

stories.headline: WNBA Finals guide: Dream-Valkyries predictions and how each team could win
stories.summary: Expect a defensive masterclass as Gabby Williams and Golden State battle Angel Reese and Atlanta for the title.
stories.byline: Michael Voepel and Alexa Philippou and Kendra Andrews and Kareem Copeland
stories.body:
After joining the WNBA as an expansion team in 2008, it took the Atlanta Dream three seasons to make the WNBA Finals. The Golden State Valkyries, who debuted in 2025, reached the Finals in their second season.

One of them will become a first-time WNBA champion before the end of the month. The best-of-seven WNBA Finals open Saturday (3:30 p.m. ET) at Chase Center in San Francisco.

The No. 2 seed Valkyries -- who will host Games 1, 2 and, if necessary, 5 and 7 -- are coming off a semifinals sweep of the defending champion Las Vegas Aces, while the No. 4 Dream swept the New York Liberty. Both those series ended Oct. 9, giving Golden State and Atlanta plenty of prep time ahead of Game 1.

Expect defense to dominate the Finals, as the Valkyries and Dream were the No. 1- and 2-rated defensive teams this season. While the Valkyries appear to be healthy, Dream guard Allisha Gray -- limited to 11 minutes in Game 1 of the semifinals because of an injury on her shooting hand (left) -- has said she is day-to-day after undergoing a recent procedure.

The Dream enter the Finals on a 10-game winning streak. Golden State won the regular-season series 3-0, but their last meeting was July 4.

Atlanta is making its fourth WNBA Finals appearance, but was swept in 2010, 2011 and 2013. Now the Dream will attempt to turn that disappointing history into an October celebration. And the Valkyries will try to join their NBA brethren Golden State Warriors as a league champion.

ESPN breaks down how the teams match up and predicts which team will hoist the trophy.

JUMP TO: GS | ATL | KEY QUESTIONS | PICKS

(2) Golden State Valkyries

How Golden State got here

The Valkyries are the first team in league history to make the WNBA Finals within the first two years of its franchise launch. They beat the Dallas Wings in three games in the best-of-three first-round series and then swept Las Vegas in the semifinals. Golden State is 5-1 this postseason, with the lone loss being Game 2 on the road against the Wings, when Arike Ogunbowale had 45 points.

The Valkyries have looked unflappable since then. In the first game of the semifinals, they held the Aces to a season-low 60 points and were plus-27 on the boards (grabbing a franchise-record 52 rebounds, including 17 offensive). In Game 3, the Valkyries rallied from their first double-digit deficit of the series to win in overtime. Gabby Williams has continued her breakout year and is the leading scorer remaining this postseason, averaging 22.7 points. Kiah Stokes is the series' leading rebounder with 9.5 per game. -- Kendra Andrews

Golden State's projected starters

G Veronica Burton (9.5 PPG)

F Kayla Thornton (10.8 PPG)

F Gabby Williams (22.7 PPG)

F Cecilia Zandalasini (8.5 PP)

C Kiah Stokes (9.5 RPG)

What we're hearing about the Valkyries

After becoming the first expansion team to make the playoffs in its inaugural season, the Valkyries were primed for greater success in Year 2 -- and aren't surprised to be here. "This is unimaginable, but for us it's so realistic," Burton said after the Valkyries swept the Aces. "It's what we expected and what we've worked for. It's what we believed in the entire year."

The players developed an immediate bond and chemistry. Part of that they credit to a clear game plan and vision from the top of the organization down, but also to the fact the roster is built of players unwanted by their previous clubs.

"A lot of us bounced around, and that's what makes it special," Thornton said. "A lot of us have been denied. ... When you bring this group together, we create something big. We do it for each other because we know what we've been through."

But as a group, the Valkyries don't have championship experience. Only four players on the roster have competed for a WNBA title: Thornton (2024), Tiffany Hayes (2023), Zandalasini (2024) and Stokes (2022, 2023, 2025). Coach Natalie Nakase was an assistant on Las Vegas' first two title teams.

"We have other WNBA champs, we have other Olympians," Williams said. "We all know how to get it done, we just now have to get it done together." -- Andrews

Why the Valkyries can win the title

Golden State's depth will be its superpower in this series. After having the best second unit in the WNBA throughout the regular season, the Valkyries' bench is scoring a league-best 32.3 points in the playoffs. The Dream's starting lineup has been the best scoring group in the postseason, but their bench averages 16.2 points. One of the biggest luxuries the Valkyries have is never knowing exactly who will go off from game to game -- but always knowing someone will.

Janelle Salaun won Sixth Player of the Year but has experienced a quiet postseason. Instead, Hayes has provided a massive spark off of the bench (13.3 PPG in the playoffs vs. 9.0 in the regular season), while Kaitlyn Chen and Kaila Charles have had momentum-swinging spurts. In Game 3 of the first round, Burton was benched after air balling consecutive shots, but the Valkyries didn't miss a beat, a luxury many teams don't have.

If the Dream are without Gray, it shrinks Atlanta's depth and gives the Valkyries' already dominant depth more of an advantage. -- Andrews

If they win, the Finals MVP will be...

This might be the easiest question in this preview. The addition of Williams took the Valkyries from a playoff team to a championship contender. She finished No. 2 in Defensive Player of the Year voting and made a defense that was already elite in 2025 (ranked No. 3 with a 99.8 defensive rating) even better (No. 1 with a 99.1 rating, with no other club being better than 103.0). During the first two rounds, she averaged 22.7 points (No. 5 of all players in the postseason), 4.8 rebounds, 4.0 assists (No. 9) and 1.7 steals (No. 6). All of those metrics have increased from the regular season, including more than 8.0 points per game. She's shooting 40.5% from behind the arc and her 2.8 3-pointers per game ranks No. 4 in the playoffs and is the highest amongst those still playing.

Williams is one of the most well-rounded players in the league, and her addition gave the Valkyries a starter who could consistently create her own shot in 1-on-1 situations, something that was missing with Golden State. She has been the biggest difference in this 2026 Valkyries squad to the point that owner Joe Lacob, after an incredible Game 1 of the semifinals, declared Williams the best player in the world. -- Kareem Copeland

If they lose, it will be because...

The Dream find cracks in the Valkyries defense. Golden State has allowed more than 81 points just once in the playoffs. In the five victories, opponents averaged 74.2 points. The Valkyries aren't just an offensive juggernaut but are four wins from holding the trophy due to a stifling defense that feeds the offense. If Dream coach Karl Smesko can figure out a way to get clean looks for Rhyne Howard, Gray (if available), Jordin Canada and DeWanna Bonner, and if Angel Reese can be successful against Stokes, that's a significant advantage. Golden State isn't exactly built for shootouts, and Atlanta has averaged 92.6 points this postseason. -- Copeland

Player ready for Finals spotlight

Stokes is familiar with the Finals, less so with the spotlight. But she deserves her time to shine. Stokes started just seven games at UConn but won three NCAA titles. The No. 11 draft pick in 2015 by New York, she stayed with the Liberty until being waived in June 2021. Two days later, Las Vegas signed her she was signed by Las Vegas. She won three WNBA championships with the Aces. Now she's a key part of the Valkyries, starting all season for them.

Stokes' commitment to doing whatever a team needs has made her a valuable veteran, and it can be easy for her to get lost in the shuffle because she doesn't score a lot (3.6 PPG in the regular season, 3.2 in playoffs). But the screens she sets, the passes she makes, plus the defense and rebounding are so big toward Golden State's success. She's coming off one of her best games of the season, with 11 points, 10 rebounds, three blocks, three assists and two steals in Golden State's 87-77 Game 3 win over the Aces. -- Michael Voepel

(4) Atlanta Dream

How Atlanta got here

The Dream have been the most dominant team in the postseason, winning five consecutive games and sweeping the Washington Mystics and New York. They defeated the Mystics by an average of 16.5 points before things became a bit more challenging against the 2024 WNBA champs. Despite losing leading scorer Gray (19.0 PPG in regular season) in Game 1 of the semis, Atlanta still won by 10. Overtime was required in Game 2, and the Dream won Games 2 and 3 by a combined five points.

Angel Reese is playing the best basketball of her career after being named Defensive Player of the Year. She is averaging 18.0 points, 8.4 rebounds, 2.2 blocks, 2.0 assists and 1.6 steals in the playoffs. Bonner has stepped into the starting lineup without Gray, whose status remains unknown for the Finals. Bonner, a veteran with 103 games of playoff experience, has been a perfect late-season addition (Atlanta signed her in late August). Canada has continued to be a defensive pest with 2.2 steals per game, which ties Howard for a 2026 postseason high, and she has increased her scoring average from 11.6 points in the regular season to 19.2 in the playoffs. -- Copeland

Atlanta's projected starters

G Jordin Canada (19.2 PPG)

G Rhyne Howard (19.2 PPG)

F Angel Reese (18.0 PPG)

F Naz Hillmon (5.2 PPG)

F DeWanna Bonner (13.2 PPG)

What we're hearing about the Dream

The Dream's 10 consecutive victories match the 2017 Sparks for the league's longest win streak entering the WNBA Finals. They are also a league-best 22-4 since a 10-point loss at home to the Portland Fire on July 11, which was their sixth loss in seven games.

The Dream credit a confluence of factors for allowing them to play their best basketball when it matters most. "I thought we had a really good [FIBA] break where we got to focus on some things," Smesko said Friday. "We had some players that got to play in the World Cup, and they all did really well. So I think they came back with a lot of confidence, and obviously adding [Bonner] added another dimension to our team.

"I just think we've been improving steadily through the season, and everybody's had a good attitude about getting better, and we've been able to play really well for a nice stretch here."

Reese and Canada have played some of the best basketball in their careers recently, but the group also attributes its hot streak to strong chemistry, something that has stood out to Bonner. "We are a really close group," she said. "I feel like I've been here since the beginning. I don't think there's a day that we don't want to come in here and come to work with each other and step on this court for each other."

With two titles apiece, Bonner and Canada are the only regular contributors who have won WNBA championships, Bonner with the Phoenix Mercury and Canada with the Seattle Storm. For Canada, those Storm championship teams boasted an off-court chemistry that translated onto the court.

"We've hung out, had team dinners, doing anything that we can to build bonds. And I think that means a lot more when you get to know a group on a deeper level outside of basketball and knowing who they are as people and what makes them go," she said. "Then in moments like this, when you're in such a heated moment or a heated series, you want to fight and you want to battle for the girl on the left and right of you." -- Alexa Philippou

Why the Dream can win the title

Even without Gray, Atlanta is the more offensively blessed team in this Finals matchup. Howard (17.7 PPG in the regular season) and Gray (19.0 PPG) are the two best offensive threats in this series and can win games on their own. Both ranked in the top 11 in scoring this season. Reese has continued to develop her offensive game, and the Dream have no problem running things through her, whether she's initiating it on the perimeter or catching it in the post. Canada's increased production adds another wrinkle into the Dream scheme while making up for the loss of Gray. Bonner, 39, is simply one of the best scorers in the history of the league, and she still has bursts that can bury an opponent.

Atlanta also loves to get out in transition off its aggressive defense that led the league in steals (9.1 per game). In the semifinals, the Dream scored 60 points off 38 turnovers in the first two games. The biggest question, which the Valkyries have answered in each round, is if the league's top defense can continue to contain some of the best offenses? -- Copeland

If they win, the Finals MVP will be...

Reese or Canada. Reese has been the motor of this squad throughout the season. She outdueled Jonquel Jones in the Liberty series, averaging 20.7 points, 7.7 rebounds, 2.3 blocks and 2.0 steals. She plays with a tenacity and toughness that reverberate through the rest of the Dream. Per Elias, her 18.0 PPG in the postseason are on pace to be the fifth-highest average in WNBA history for a player making the Finals in their first playoff run.

Canada has been referred to as the head of the snake in Atlanta and has been its X factor this postseason: Her 19.2 points per game in the playoffs are well above her regular season average (11.6 points) and are tied with Howard for best on the team. She's achieving that with stellar efficiency -- 51.6% from the field (33 of 64), 50% from 3-point range (12 of 24) and at the free throw line (18 of 18) -- all while quarterbacking the offense (8.8 assists) and defense (2.2 steals per game). -- Phillipou

If they lose, it will be because...

Atlanta can't generate offense off Golden State turnovers and gets hurt by its lack of depth. The Dream's defensive pressure makes them elite at forcing turnovers and turning them into points: They were No. 1 in the league in steals per game (9.1) and points off turnovers in the regular season (18.1), and No. 2 in fast-break points (11.9). But Golden State excels in taking care of the ball: During the regular season, the Valkyries' 11.5 turnovers per game were fewest in the league, and in the playoffs that number is even lower (10.3, second to Dream's 9.0).

The Dream are much less deeper than the Valkyries. Golden State's bench averaged 35.9 points in the regular season versus Atlanta's 17.9 PPG, one of the lowest marks in the league -- and that will be exacerbated even more if Gray cannot play. Golden State's litany of options could prove to be too much for an Atlanta squad that relies significantly on its starting five and could be without its top scorer. -- Phillipou

Player ready for Finals spotlight

Bonner left the Mercury to try to win a championship in what could be the final year of her career, and she's now four wins away. Most of the Dream players are relatively inexperienced on this stage. But Bonner -- who holds the league record for playoff games -- is not, and her leadership will be crucial for Atlanta to navigate the ups and downs of a seven-game series. Her offensive firepower (13.2 PPG in the playoffs) will be even more necessary for Atlanta if Gray can't play. -- Phillipou

Four key questions

How do the teams match up?

Atlanta has been great at forcing turnovers (17.2 per game) in its first two playoff series and converting those into points. That will be harder against Golden State, which has averaged just 9.2 turnovers in the playoffs. The Valkyries and the Dream (8.4) are the only two teams to average fewer than 10 turnovers in this postseason. Like so many things in this series, this is a strength vs. strength matchup.

That leads us to how the teams guard each other. Reese was the Defensive Player of the Year but A'ja Wilson is one of the best defensive players in WNBA history, and the Valkyries still figured out ways to get shots they wanted against her and the Aces in the semifinals -- and then convert enough of them.

The Valkyries' first two playoff opponents have been good preparation for facing the Dream in terms of how much Dallas and Las Vegas were able to challenge Golden State's defense. The Valkyries rose to that challenge. But neither the Wings nor the Aces presented as good a defense as Atlanta brings.

So that should end up being the biggest key: Will the Valkyries find enough offensive success to win the championship? -- Voepel

What is the series X factor?

It could be health. Gray is one of the best players in the league. Even though the Dream won the semifinals with her playing only briefly before her Game 1 injury, she is a big absence. The Valkyries would have a different challenge guarding the Dream with Gray on the floor. Adding to her offensive repertoire, she's a very good defender and one of the most experienced players on the court. Gray is used to stepping up in big moments. If there is any way she can return to the Dream with some effectiveness, it could make a difference in this series. If not, the Valkyries' depth edge remains a key factor. -- Voepel

Ballhalla will boast 18,000-plus fans. The Dream aren't playing at their usual home arena. How much will home-court advantage be a factor?

As someone who has spent the better part of the past six months watching games in Ballhalla, there are very few home-court advantages such as what the Valkyries have at Chase Center. It isn't just that they have a raucous crowd or they've sold out every home game the past two seasons. The energy -- the rowdiness, the joy, the party -- makes it feel almost like a basketball utopia. Golden State went a league-best 17-5 at home during the regular season and it has yet to lose a game in San Francisco during these playoffs. The noise inside Chase Center is deafening, and it'll only get louder in the Finals. The Bay Area is built for playoff -- and championship -- basketball.

This isn't to say that Atlanta's home court won't be rocking. Adjusting the schedule to allow the Dream to play at State Farm Arena (which seats up to 17,000) rather than the 3,500-seat Gateway Arena was critical for the team and the league. While this isn't the Dream's usual homecourt, it's not unfamiliar. They played six regular-season games at State Farm and played all three postseason home contests there. There's a reason this was the only alternate venue the Dream wanted to play Finals games in. But for the Dream to win the Finals, they have to win at least one game on the road. That has been difficult in Ballhalla. -- Andrews

Will Atlanta's 0-3 record against Golden State in the regular season matter? What did we learn from those meetings?

Teams sometimes downplay prior results for a presumed strategic or motivational advantage. In this case, those games were so long ago, they don't have much bearing on what we're about to see.

All three meetings happened during an 11-day span from June 24 to July 4, with the first two games at Golden State and the third at Atlanta. It was during the worst stretch of the summer for the Dream, as they lost a season-high five games in a row.

In the first meeting, Atlanta was held to a season-low 66 points and shot 39% from the field, with Golden State making 15 3-pointers to the Dream's four. Back at Chase Center two days later, the Dream struggled even more from the field (34%). Atlanta got closer, but Golden State made enough free throws in the final minute to prevail.

After road losses at Seattle and Washington, the Dream took on Golden State again, this time in Atlanta. Once more, the Dream didn't shoot well (39%), although Gray, Howard and Reese combined for 58 points.

Atlanta didn't have Bonner for any of these games, and as a late addition, she has been a big difference-maker. Neither team is going to look back too much on what happened between them in the regular season as indicative of what's going to take place next. -- Voepel

WNBA Finals picks

Kendra Andrews: Golden State in 7. It's odd that the No. 2 team in the standings still feels like the underdog, but the Valkyries have proved time and again to never count them out. With a matchup of the top two defensive teams in the league, this series will be a slugfest, and the championship might come down to who can hit the last shot (or make the last stop). Not enough credit has been given to what the Valkyries have done on both sides of the ball this postseason. Watching what they did to the Aces showed they have another gear they can get to, and that will be crucial in this series.

Kareem Copeland: Atlanta in 7. The Dream have been held to fewer than 85 points just once since Aug. 28. Especially if Gray is back, the Valkyries will be challenged to shut down that offense four times in seven games. The Aces were short-handed and were more of a half-court-centered team on offense. Golden State wants to run off defensive stops, but Atlanta also wants to run as often as possible, even when taking the ball out of the net. A fast, up-tempo game would seem to favor the Dream.

Alexa Philippou: Golden State in 6. After seeing Atlanta dismantle the Liberty up close, the Dream were my pick to win it all as the team that has played the best basketball in the league by the end of the season. But my predictions have not aged well as we've progressed in the playoffs, so I'll go with the Valkyries continuing to make history and benefitting from their enormous home-court advantage at Ballhalla, including in a potential Game 7.

Michael Voepel: Golden State in 7. This isn't a fluke Finals matchup. The Valkyries were the No. 1 team in our final ESPN Power Rankings, and the Dream were fourth. Now they really do look like the best two teams after five months of physically and mentally grueling play. Both have played championship-worthy basketball in the postseason. Both coaches have been impressive in their preparation and adjustments. This pick is for two things that go Golden State's way: depth and home-court advantage for the series.

stories.headline: Down 3-0 in NLCS, are Dodgers done in 2026 MLB playoffs?
stories.summary: Can the Dodgers make history ... or are the Brewers about to dethrone the two-time defending champs?
stories.body:
Just one MLB team has come back from a 3-0 deficit to win a postseason series.

Can the Los Angeles Dodgers become the second?

The two-time defending World Series champs are down 3-0 to the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series. To return to the Fall Classic, they will need to channel their manager's former team -- the 2004 Boston Red Sox, who, with help from a timely Dave Roberts steal, mounted a historic ALCS comeback against the New York Yankees.

So how did L.A. get here? Can the Dodgers dig themselves out of this hole? Are the Brewers really this good? We asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Alden Gonzalez and David Schoenfield those questions and more.

Are the Dodgers done or can they still get this series back to Milwaukee?

Doolittle: I can't see them getting back to Milwaukee. Maybe the Dodgers can avoid a sweep, but the Brewers will not be looking past Game 4 and, man, L.A. looked really disheartened over the last couple of innings in Game 3. The end for the Dodgers is nigh.

Schoenfield: I suppose Roberts could put his stolen base from Game 4 of the 2004 ALCS on loop on the TVs in the clubhouse in an attempt to inspire his team and remind it that there is at least one team in MLB playoff history that has won a series after losing the first three games. "I've lived it," he said after the game.

But the Brewers are young and athletic and fast and run everything down in the outfield and steal bases and are the ones putting together memory-making 11-pitch home run at-bats. The Dodgers look old. Sure, the Red Sox came back in 2004; but they were fighting for an elusive championship. The Dodgers already have their rings and might not have the fight in them at this point.

How surprised are you that this series is 3-0 Brewers?

Schoenfield: In our LCS predictions, most of us at ESPN picked the Brewers to win -- 13 out of 15. That made the series appear more lopsided than most of us thought. I'm sure most believed the series would go at least six, and most likely seven games, especially considering the strength of the Dodgers' rotation and Yoshinobu Yamamoto's recent postseason success. Now the Dodgers might not even get to another Yamamoto start. So, yes: surprised.

Gonzalez: As one of the two who didn't pick the Brewers, very much so. It was only a year ago that the Dodgers swept the Brewers out of the NLCS, outscoring them 15-4 in the process. And while this is a different year with different circumstances, at the end of the day, the Dodgers were going to trot out four aces in Tarik Skubal, Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. In other words, they would have the starting pitching advantage in at least three of the first four games and potentially all of them. I felt that might tip the odds in their favor. And the last thing I thought was that it might result in them getting swept.

What has been L.A.'s biggest problem in this series?

Doolittle: It would be hard to make an argument that the Dodgers have put their best foot forward, but in the end, their biggest problem is the Brewers. The Brewers were the best team in baseball during the season, they have been the best team in the playoffs, and they have been the best team in the NLCS. The series is what it is not because of the Dodgers, but because of the Brewers.

Gonzalez: They can't hit. More specifically, they can't hit with men on base. The Dodgers got the leadoff man on in three of the first five innings in Game 3 and never scored him. They got a big hit courtesy of Will Smith's two-run double in the sixth, but that was it. The Dodgers are batting .146 with men on base in this series, 147 points lower than the Brewers. For the playoffs, in every situation, they've produced a .572 OPS -- ranked 240th among the 246 teams that have played at least seven games in a single postseason. It's bad.

What has impressed you most about the Brewers so far?

Doolittle: There's a lot, but when you think about past teams that have won it all, a hot bullpen can really propel a team all the way through. The Royals in 2015. The Reds in 1990. The Braves in 2021. The Brewers are a strong team in every department but right now, it's that lights-out bullpen that really makes them tough to beat.

Schoenfield: The quality of their at-bats. Jake Bauers' dramatic home run came on the 11th pitch from Snell -- making him only the sixth player in the pitch counting era (since 1988) to hit a postseason home run on the 11th pitch or later. These at-bats shouldn't be a surprise. The Brewers had the best walk rate in the majors in the regular season. They had the lowest chase rate. They were second in batting average and first in OPS with runners in scoring position. Oh, and despite their supposed lack of power, fifth in home runs.

What is one ray of hope Dodgers fans can hang onto down 3-0?

Schoenfield: Just win Game 4. The Dodgers will have Glasnow and all their primary relievers -- Tanner Scott, Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Edwin Diaz -- well-rested after none of them pitched Wednesday. Heck, Diaz hasn't even pitched in the series yet. The Brewers will be going with a bullpen game. So, win Game 4, and then you have Skubal and Yamamoto lined up for Games 5 and 6 -- just like the Red Sox in 2004 had Pedro Martinez and Curt Schilling. Then, in Game 7, it's back to Snell and Robert Gasser. The Dodgers look cooked, but they haven't turned the grill off just yet.

Gonzalez: Max Muncy put it best: "At the beginning of this year, we set out to do something historic. It looks like we're going to have to make a little more history along the way if we want to accomplish that. That's the task ahead of us. We still have the pitching staff to be able to do it." To echo Dave's point, the pitching -- the starting pitching in particular -- is what should offer hope. Glasnow, Skubal, Yamamoto and Snell are all capable of shutting down an opposing lineup and winning a game almost singlehandedly. They're all going to have to do that -- four games in a row, likely in that order.

stories.headline: 10 people who will define the NBA season: Zion, Kawhi, Kyrie
stories.summary: With the NBA season just days away, let's take stock of the most important coaches, execs and players worth monitoring.
stories.body:
The 2025-26 NBA season is less than a week away, and while there are so many storylines surrounding the Philadelphia 76ers' present and the future of the NBA champion New York Knicks, there are several intriguing narratives around the league.

In some instances, it could take all season to shake out, while others could have a fate determined in the first quarter of the campaign.

Either way, here are 10 important people at all levels of the game who bear watching, starting with a No. 1 pick who is still looking to make his playoff debut.

Zion Williamson, New Orleans Pelicans
Why he's interesting: It's now or never, period.

Williamson's 62 games last season were the second most of his career, trailing only the 70 he played in 2022-23. His stretch of playing 52 of 53 games from Dec. 14 to April 5 was the longest such span of his career. The Pelicans were 21-31 during that time, as the team had a litany of players in and out through the season while trying to develop rookies Jeremy Fears and Derik Queen.

This is Year 8 for the 2019 No. 1 pick. The league moves fast, and Williamson's contract for 2027-28 is not guaranteed. Pelicans GM Troy Weaver previously went through the painstaking process of a Pistons rebuild at the start of the decade, with no assets to accrue draft capital, but that's not the case here. The new regime resisted wholesale changes last season, and they hope new coach Jamahl Mosley will have the same effect J.B. Bickerstaff had in Detroit three years ago before they make any drastic moves.

Williamson has the most credentials, but also the most questions. Apparently, he's come into camp in great shape, working plenty with assistant coach God Shammgod over the summer.

Doug Christie, Sacramento Kings
Why he's interesting: The bar isn't high.

There's no mandate for the Kings to make the playoffs with the current roster, and the front office has stated it would not saddle itself with win-now moves that jeopardize the future. Zach LaVine is on an expiring deal, and who knows how Domantas Sabonis, who has two years left on the extension he signed in 2023, fits into the future.

But Christie has yet to put an imprint on this roster as far as style of play, which is something Kings GM Scott Perry is big on. If Christie can put promising rookie point guard Darius Acuff Jr. in positions to be an elite lead performer, it will certainly be a feather in his cap while the roster starts to take shape. If it's another nondescript 22-win season with no discernible on-court quality, things could get tricky for the well-liked Christie.

LaMelo Ball, Minnesota Timberwolves
Why he's intriguing: The Timberwolves aren't strangers to big moves, going back to acquiring Rudy Gobert from the Utah Jazz for a cache of future picks and trading Karl-Anthony Towns to the Knicks two years ago, following their first trip to the Western Conference finals in 20 years. Now Tim Connelly is remaking the roster, bringing in the uber-talented Ball to alleviate pressure on Anthony Edwards, who wound up taking on a heavy share of facilitating duties during the past couple of seasons.

Ball, who seems to be getting along famously with Edwards in the early returns, is tasked in two ways. First, and most importantly, Ball is facing high-stakes, high-pressure basketball for the first time in his NBA career. For his first six seasons with the Charlotte Hornets, the play-in tournament was the high-water mark. Second, can he stay healthy? He has played 70 games twice in his career and joins a team that wants to elevate itself to the Oklahoma City Thunder/San Antonio Spurs tier of the West.

Micah Nori and Ja Morant, Portland Trail Blazers
Why they're intriguing: The only player-coach combo on this list is notable, even if they're not joined at the hip. Nori, the highly regarded assistant in Minnesota, took this job under less than desirable circumstances. Only the first year of his contract is guaranteed, with team options for the second and third year -- a deal National Basketball Coaches Association president J.B. Bickerstaff called a "slap in the face." Trail Blazers governor Tom Dundon has already caught flak for his cheap practices, and it seems like Nori is in a lose-lose situation.

That's where Morant comes in. It's been years since he was an All-Star (2022 and 2023), let alone a future face of the league. The trade from the Memphis Grizzlies was a merciful end, but going to Portland means there's a franchise legend at the same position returning from an Achilles injury: Damian Lillard. Jrue Holiday is still there along with Scoot Henderson. Where does Morant fit in, not just on this team but in the league at large?

His game hasn't developed with an outside shot, and his body has been beaten up by injuries that have limited him to just 79 games in the past three seasons. He's due $42.1 million and $44.8 million in the next two years and will be 29 when free agency hits.

Is Portland a fertile ground for a hard reset? Or are matters far too complicated for either Nori or Morant to truly succeed?

Anthony Davis, Washington Wizards
Why he's intriguing: It's been a while since we've seen Davis as an impact player -- he has played a total of 71 games in the past two seasons -- so he has something to prove. Davis has yet to play a game for the Wizards and, unlike Trae Young, didn't get a contract extension. So Davis is entering a potential contract year -- he holds a $62.7 million player option for 2027-28 -- in a place he didn't choose, making his situation all the more interesting. He's a veteran on a team with No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa, a 20-point, 10-assist threat in Young and 2024 No. 2 pick Alex Sarr, who has shown more than a little promise through two seasons.

The relationship between Davis and the Wizards seems to be going well, and he will want to put his best foot forward to secure his future as he turns 34 in March. If he's healthy, Davis is still one of the more versatile bigs in the league and a Hall of Famer the day he becomes eligible. If he's healthy, he could be a coveted player should he and the Wizards not come to terms on a contract extension. Both sides understand it's a business; it's just a matter of how this plays out -- and how long it will take for clarity.

Karl-Anthony Towns, New York Knicks
Why he's intriguing: It seems fairly obvious; his talks with the Knicks regarding an extension have hung over the organization since the Knicks won their first title in 53 years. Talks have been cut off after Towns found the Knicks' offer of $200 million over four years to be unsatisfactory. That figure is not only $76 million less than his potential max of $276 million over four seasons, but it also represents a pay cut from his current salary of $57 million. Like Davis, he's armed with a player option for next season at $61 million that the second apron-conscious Knicks have to be aware of.

One of the reasons Towns was traded from Minnesota a couple of years ago was because of his salary and Minnesota's desire to get from under the second apron in its first year. One wonders if that plays in his mind and heart as the Knicks go for a repeat. Is everything on the table if the Knicks are true to their word of not negotiating during the season?

The Knicks were one band, one sound during their run to the NBA Finals last season, and repeating is tougher than ever in today's league. How will they manage it? How will Towns, who sacrificed last season and is now being asked to sacrifice again, go beyond his expectations?

Kenny Atkinson, Cleveland Cavaliers
Why he's intriguing: Perhaps we've made too much fun of his comments during the Eastern Conference finals, where he told the media that "analytically" they had won two of the three games against the Knicks even though they were on the way to being swept. It obscured the best season and playoff run Cleveland has had that wasn't headlined by LeBron James in over 30 years. But the Cavs looked emotionally and physically spent going into that series with the Knicks, so was that the maximum Atkinson could've gotten from his team? And with the Eastern Conference looking improved from top to bottom, where do the Cavaliers fit in? Can Atkinson truly unlock Evan Mobley, a No. 1 talent who's the third option in this setup?

Donovan Mitchell re-signed for the max, and James Harden agreed to a three-year deal as he enters his age-37 season with a lot of miles on his body and legs.

The Cavaliers acquired Peyton Watson from the Denver Nuggets via a sign-and-trade deal, but is that enough to keep up? And can Atkinson shake off those comments and perception to keep the Cavaliers in the upper echelon?

Kyrie Irving, Dallas Mavericks
Why he's intriguing: Because he's a wizard with the ball, the perfect shot-creating guard who barely needs a sliver of space to get a shot off with either hand, unafraid to take the big shots in the big moments ... and we have no idea how his ACL surgery will affect his game, considering he hasn't been on the floor in live action in 19 months.

Irving found ways to excel next to LeBron James in Cleveland, Kevin Durant in Brooklyn and Luka Doncic in Dallas, meaning he should have little trouble figuring out how to work with Cooper Flagg, who stands to take a big leap in Year 2. There's new leadership in Dallas, Masai Ujiri as team president and first-year coach Dusty May, and there haven't been whispers about Irving's current fit.

Irving will turn 35 in March, and he has a player option for 2027-28 at $42.4 million and could be a coveted veteran for more than a few contenders if that's where his fate takes him.

But it's long been said he's comfortable in Dallas, and that shouldn't be taken lightly. Some of his most productive and efficient play has been with the Mavericks, so it shouldn't be assumed he will be on the way out. Either way, a return to the court for a spellbinding performer is noteworthy.

Jon Horst, Milwaukee Bucks
Why he's intriguing: Travis Scott's "Butterfly Effect" -- Giannis Antetokounmpo's song of choice once he scored at Fiserv Forum -- won't be playing there anymore after his trade to the Miami Heat. But the butterfly effect of that move will continue to ripple.

Unless your name is Sam Presti, trading away your franchise star is usually signing your own pink slip as opposed to being able to engineer the next phase of team building. Horst did a masterful job in building the team that became an NBA champion in 2021, then used every creative lever he could to keep Antetokounmpo happy until the relationship ran its course.

The return for the franchise star and Bobby Portis was three first-round picks, Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Kel'el Ware. Lillard's waive-and-stretch deal is still on the books until 2029-30 at $21 million per season.

And there's the matter of the league's investigation to their signing of Gary Trent Jr. for salary cap circumvention. If the LA Clippers case is any guide -- and nobody's comparing the actual severity of the two instances -- the NBA will look at this very seriously.

Will Horst still have the chance to rebuild the Bucks into another contender?

Kawhi Leonard, Toronto Raptors
Why he's intriguing: The yearlong investigation surrounding Leonard receiving impermissible benefits from the Clippers is over. He wasn't suspended but forced to repay restitution of $700,000 in impermissible benefits and was traded back to his preferred destination of Toronto, where he helped the Raptors win their only NBA title in 2019.

He would probably prefer if nobody asked anything about his Clippers experience, and the Raptors don't care what happened in the past seven years -- handing him a lucrative three-year extension upon arrival, in hopes that history will repeat itself.

The Raptors were a first-round out last year but have talented players, even after trading Brandon Ingram and Gradey Dick to the Clippers. Leonard, if healthy, can make it all fit in a crowded Eastern Conference. But can he be trusted, just to stay on the floor?

Last year was one of his best, even amid the controversy, averaging nearly 28 points on ridiculous 50-39-89 splits. But he's 35, and there's all that physical baggage.

"I want to love Kawhi because he's an incredible talent," a high-ranking Western Conference exec told ESPN. "However, he doesn't abide by the rules of the game. Which is to be available. If he played 70 games, he's a top-three player. I'd take my chances with him."

stories.headline: Man United 'a circus' amid Lisandro Martínez rant - Roy Keane
stories.summary: Roy Keane has branded Manchester United a "circus" following Lisandro Martínez's outburst against the club's hierarchy.
stories.body:
Roy Keane has branded Manchester United a "circus" following Lisandro Martínez's outburst against the club's hierarchy.

Argentina defender Martínez accused the club of lacking ambition and questioned their summer recruitment after Tuesday night's 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid.

Former United defender Gary Neville said Martínez's comments amounted to a direct attack on his team-mates and suggested senior players would be "absolutely fuming," while ex-captain Keane described the remarks as symptomatic of the "chaos" at Old Trafford.

"They're obviously not together," Keane said of the club, speaking on The Overlap's Stick to Football podcast. "It is chaotic there from the top to the bottom. We go there on match days and I don't like the feeling around the club.

"It just seems chaotic -- statements can reflect it. It was chaotic with how they got to (Michael] Carrick as their manager.

"We said from day one there were better options out there, and maybe the players are looking at there's better options as players out there. It's chaos, it's like a circus."

Lisandro Martínez rant riles Man United legends

Martínez hit out at director of football Jason Wilcox and the United board in a caustic interview amid the club's worst start to a league season since 1986.

Neville and Keane shared some of Martínez's concerns about the state of the club.

However, both questioned the World Cup winner's individual performances and whether he had sufficient standing to make such comments.

"When Martínez says they should have brought more players in, he's directly attacking his team-mates," said Neville.

"If I was Bruno Fernandes and I was Harry Maguire and the other senior players, I'd be absolutely fuming with him because you're basically saying that some of us shouldn't be here and we should be bringing more players in.

"That's what I think he's saying."

Martínez attempted to take the sting out of the situation in a statement issued on Instagram on Wednesday.

"I don't think it will be a big falling out," said Keane. "Because I think we've question marks over this dressing room anyway.

"I don't think there's enough characters, enough men in there. We know that.

"But I don't see him as a senior player at Man United; I see him as a centre-half who's making lots of mistakes."

- Martínez exposes Man United's harsh reality: Blame lies with top brass, not Carrick

- Transfer rumors, news: Martínez's future at Man United in doubt after bust-up

- Wayne Rooney criticises Cristiano Ronaldo over Portugal walkout: 'Wrong in every sense'

United have not publicly responded to the remarks but were assessing their defender's comments before deciding whether to take disciplinary action, sources told ESPN.

"I thought it was really strange to have a go at Jason Wilcox, not because he's above criticism but the budget is not going to be set by Jason Wilcox; the budget is going to be set by the owners," said Neville.

"It was obvious they needed more defenders. He [Martínez] would probably be one of the first on the chopping block if players were actually brought in."

Information from ESPN's Rob Dawson, and the Press Association, contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Franco Colapinto urges fans to stop 'attacking' Formula 1 drivers on social media
stories.summary: Franco Colapinto has urged his supporters to stop attacking other Formula 1 drivers and personnel on social media.
stories.body:
Franco Colapinto has urged his supporters to stop attacking other Formula 1 drivers and personnel on social media.

The Alpine driver is in his first full season on the circuit and commands a strong following online. In recent months, his supporters have gone after drivers like Pierre Gasly and Lando Norris.

His teammate Gasly was targeted by fans after preventing Colapinto from overtaking him in the Madrid Grand Prix, with the Frenchman revealing his family members and girlfriend had also been subjected to abuse.

Norris suffered the wrath of Colapinto's fans for suggesting that the Argentine doesn't deserve a spot on the grid after he caused a crash in Baku at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Norris later rolled back his comments.

These incidents forced Colapinto to address his supporters in a social media post.

"I probably should have spoken to all of you sooner, but this is something that needs to be addressed, something we need to change and improve," he said.

"I will always be grateful, and I genuinely feel incredibly fortunate to have had you all supporting me from the very beginning. I'm grateful for all the support you give me, for how you help me achieve results, and for how you constantly push me to aim higher.

"You help me and the team achieve our results, race after race, day after day, as we train and try to improve. And I'm genuinely grateful for all of that.

"I know it makes you incredibly proud when things go well for me, when I score points for myself and the team. And I have always been very grateful for that support.

- F1 still planning Middle East finale amid Kimi Antonelli title uncertainty - sources

- Christian Horner: Mercedes' Toto Wolff has it 'easy' at the moment

"But sometimes, we go too far.

"Instead of supporting me, we end up criticising people and attacking other drivers, other colleagues, my teammates, my mechanics, my engineers -- people I work with every single day.

"I know you think you're defending me, but you're actually doing the opposite. You're not helping me or my future."

stories.headline: The UFC's flyweights are hot again - is Lone'er Kavanagh the next star?
stories.summary: Could a breakout win at UFC 333 propel Britain's Lone'er Kavanagh into the flyweight title picture?
stories.body:
The fighting life of a UFC flyweight was once an unenvied one.

Constant uncertainty over the future of the division, a lack of big pay-per-view interest and an unfortunate routine of far too many fighters getting cut for the weight class to sustain itself were just some of the problems that characterised the modern era. UFC president Dana White put it in simple terms, saying after Demetrious Johnson's UFC exit in 2018 that "people didn't care" about the flyweights. Even Olympic gold medalist and former two-division champion Henry Cejudo struggled to see how the flyweight division would continue as a part of the UFC, with his own brash persona and entertaining title defences pivotal to maintaining awareness of the division.

Much has changed since the days of Cejudo though, and the flyweights now have a genuine claim to being one of the most exciting divisions in the whole of the UFC. And one man at the forefront of that charge is another promising fighting talent from across the Atlantic, with England's Lone'er Kavanagh enjoying a rise like few others this past year.

He accepted a short-notice fight against ex-champion Brandon Moreno in the lion's den of Mexico City in March and produced one of the most stunning UFC upsets in recent memory, taking the unanimous decision win in front of a hostile crowd. Kavanagh was unranked before that fight and despite more recently losing to Brandon Royval at UFC 329, he remains just a win away from breaking into the flyweight title conversation. Taking on Royval on the night of Conor McGregor's return in Las Vegas in July, Kavanagh was submitted but earned the fight of the night on one of the promotion's most-watched recent cards in a back-and-forth slugfest. The 27-year-old's exciting style and high ceiling was on show that evening and will be again when he faces Ramazonbek Temirov on what is remarkably just his second high-profile numbered event at UFC 333 on Oct. 24.

"Thinking back to certain moments [in Mexico City], it was like a rollercoaster, it was a sick opportunity and I'm glad I did it and my team backed me to do it," Kavanagh tells ESPN.

"[Royval was] another step on the journey, losing is never fun, no matter what stage you're at whether you're at the top or at any point of your career but unfortunately sometimes you have to learn like that -- learning on the go, that's what we're doing right now.

"I believe I've got the best team around me so I truly believe with this team I can make it all the way to the top and that's the plan, that's the aim.

"I'm always trying to work on things from every fight. Unfortunately, you learn a lot more when you lose."

For Kavanagh, the lights have quickly turned brighter. Like many of his British counterparts in the UFC, he was made in Cage Warriors, the organisation that can take credit for the likes of McGregor, Paddy Pimblett and Tom Aspinall. From there, a first round knockout on Dana White's Contender Series saw the journey in the big time begin. His first professional defeat came in the UFC against the experienced Charles Johnson, but that was quickly forgotten with the Moreno heist that saw his stock in the game skyrocket. Kavanagh's front-footed, devious style stemming from his kickboxing roots has even earned him praise from one of the greatest to ever step in the octagon with a Jon Jones Facetime after that UFC Mexico win leaving him "starstruck."

"Your Muay Thai is beautiful, your kicks, they don't show at all. They have no telegraph. It's so nice," Jones said to Kavanagh.

It is a style that was born at London's Great Britain Top Team (GBTT), where alongside UFC veteran Nathaniel Wood and fellow prospect Shanelle Dyer, Kavanagh has honed his craft, going from a five-time K1 kickboxing champion to now potentially a statement win away from challenging for UFC gold under British MMA trailblazer Brad Pickett. And that too in a division where the competition is possibly as fierce as it has ever been. Royval, Tatsuro Tairo, Manuel Kape, Asu Almabayev and bona fide flyweight royalty Alexandre Pantoja make up the spine of a group of challengers that Kananagh finds himself a part of.

Joshua Van's UFC 331 title defence ended any doubts about his validity as champion, with a dominant win over Pantoja, and at just 24-years-old he looks set for a stint at the top -- where Kavanagh aspires to be. But first, No. 7 ranked, one below Kavanagh, and unbeaten in the UFC, the explosive Temirov is one of the toughest challenges the Englishman has faced in his career, and in a weight class as deep as the flyweights, back-to-back losses would see Kavanagh fall mercilessly down the pecking order -- the stakes are high at UFC 333.

"I think the flyweight division is the best division at the moment. It's forever changing," Kavanagh says. "There are so many young up and comers but there are also so many people that have been around for so long. So it's got a good mixture of everything and to be honest, just excited to be a part of it - it's sick being a flyweight at this time.

"I'm a very 'one fight at a time' kind of person, I'll always look at what's in front of me and then what's next but I think it would be an exciting fight either way, [Joshua] Van vs. Lon."

Born in London to an Irish father and Chinese mother, Kavanagh wears his heritage on his sleeve with his name Lone'er translating to "Little Dragon" in English. He credits his mum for pushing him into MMA, a decision that has since paid dividends.

Kavanagh is now set to be a part of a main card alongside two title fights at the Etihad Arena in Abu Dhabi. In his way, Uzbekistan's Temirov is coming in red hot on the back of a first-round finish against Steve Erceg, he last tasted defeat in an MMA bout seven years ago and has never been knocked out.

"I haven't seen all the fighters just fighting like me. Just striking punches, just making knockouts. But my punches will just kill them all," Temirov told the UFC.

The kickboxer is aware of the danger that Temirov carries but also the opportunity up for grabs.

"I think a win there puts me right back up there. He's a dangerous opponent. He's got some good wins under him, a lot of wins, but I think a win against him puts me right back up at the top. [I'm] always looking for a finish," Kavanagh said.

"His main weapons are his heavy hands, and that excites me. I love fights like that and I think it's a good fight for me. Hopefully [another fight of the night], I'm looking for more performances of the night."

As is now customary with Kavanagh's UFC bouts, his throwdown against the formidable Temirov is one not to be missed. With the top of the flyweight division so deep he will want to turn all the excitement surrounding him into consistency to earn a shot at Van's belt, that journey will take its latest step in a treacherous division.

And as Bruce Buffer introduces both fighters, perhaps there will be something for the UFC bosses and fans alike to take away before a single punch is even thrown. That all these years after Cejudo and Johnson have been and gone, the flyweights are box office property once again.

stories.headline: AFL trade and free agency grades - Every club's report card from the 2026 transfer period
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL trade and free agency period is over. Some teams improved, some stagnated, and others, well, got worse. Here's how every team fared over the last two weeks.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL trade and free agency period is complete. Some teams improved, some have stagnated, and others, well, seemed to have gotten worse.

READ: Every player move from the 2026 off-season

Here's how every team fared over the last two weeks:

Adelaide
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Jordon Butts, Luke Pedlar

2026 draft selections: 15, 32, 35, 43, 56, 92

I'm not sure what the Crows' gameplan was this trade and free agency period, but it's fair to say the club sat on its hands and did next to nothing. Losing key defender Jordon Butts to the Bulldogs obviously weakens them, while just one draft selection inside the top 30 is unlikely to provide much immediate support. Adelaide's list profile remains fine, and maybe they will surprise us all in 2027, but you just get the sense so many other clubs have passed them by over the last two weeks.

Grade: F

Brisbane
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Lachie Neale, Sam Marshall, Will McLachlan, Keidean Coleman

2026 draft selections: 21, 27, 28, 45, 79, 97

The Lions were the biggest winners of last year's off-season (and season!), but this year was a different story. All year it seemed a formality they would lose the services of dual Brownlow Medal winner Lachie Neale, who ultimately signed with Collingwood as a free agent. They also waved goodbye to Keidean Coleman and Sam Marshall, two players who had struggled to crack the best 23 of late. No picks inside the top 20 would be concerning for 17 other clubs, but the Lions still have so much young talent at their disposal and are primed to challenge again in 2027.

Grade: C-

Carlton
Incoming: Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield

Outgoing: Hudson O'Keeffe, Flynn Riley

2026 draft selections: 13, 18, 31, 50, 61, 72, 90

The Blues addressed two areas of weakness this off-season. The addition of free agent Joel Amartey provides spearhead Harry McKay with a stable forward line partner, while the Lachie Whitfield signing offers run, experience, and a kick-first option off halfback, the perfect piece to fit into Josh Fraser's system. Carlton really didn't give up much to land Whitfield, either. And barring Essendon taking a stab at talented father-son prospect Cody Walker with pick No. 1, the club has also ensured it has enough draft capital to match any bids that will come for him.

Grade: A

Collingwood
Incoming: Lachie Neale, Jesse Hogan, Flynn Riley

Outgoing: Scott Pendlebury

2026 draft selections: 11, 30, 67, 68, 70, 88

The Magpies had been crying out for a true inside midfielder, and they landed arguably the best in the competition in Lachie Neale. The two-time Brownlow Medal winner is an elite ball winner and clearance player, and should perfectly complement superstar Nick Daicos. Collingwood also signed Jesse Hogan, a man that won the Coleman Medal just two years ago, and gave up virtually nothing for him. The loss of champion Scott Pendlebury obviously stings, but you have to feel this club is in a stronger position now than it was two weeks ago.

Grade: A

Essendon
Incoming: Jack Bowes, Keidean Coleman

Outgoing: Zach Merrett, Jordan Ridley

2026 draft selections: 1, 17, 25, 80

Former skipper Zach Merrett finally got his wish of a fresh start at the Hawks, while fellow experienced player Jordan Ridley also departs the club for the Cats. The additions of Jack Bowes and Keidean Coleman are fine, but are either going to be difference makers in a side that's been languishing at the bottom of the ladder for several years? I'm not so sure. The only saving grace for the Bombers is that they hold pick No. 1. They simply have to make the most of that selection.

Grade: D

Fremantle
Incoming: Dom Bedendo

Outgoing: Nathan O'Driscoll

2026 draft selections: 19, 40, 60, 63, 78, 96

The Dockers were incredibly quiet during the trade and free agency window, but that's not exactly a bad thing. Remember, if not for Will Ashcroft and Logan Morris, Fremantle win the 2026 premiership. There was absolutely no reason for the Dockers to panic and overpay for someone after their Grand Final heartbreak, instead, this club, with its plethora of youth and talent, should feel as if it can contend for years to come. Trust the process and go again in 2027.

Grade: C

Geelong
Incoming: Toby Greene, Jordan Ridley, Rowan Marshall

Outgoing: Jack Bowes

2026 draft selections: 36, 57, 62, 75, 93

Every year the Cats just find a way to bring big names through the door, and 2026 was no exception. Rowan Marshall was tipped to join 12 months ago and finally makes the move from St Kilda to bolster the club's ruck stocks. Toby Greene adds class, experience, and unrivalled goal-kicking nous to the forward line. Jordan Ridley is a stable and still wildly underrated defensive asset. The best part? To land this trio the club only had to give up midfield depth piece Jack Bowes, and some draft capital. They won't be much of a feature at the upcoming draft, but they don't have to be. These Cats are in win-now mode.

Grade: A

Gold Coast Suns
Incoming: Scott Pendlebury, Aidan Schubert, Sam Butler

Outgoing: Ben King

2026 draft selections: 8, 85

Scott Pendlebury might be a champion of the game, but there's no denying the Suns just got worse. The addition of 38-year-old Pendlebury doesn't outweigh the seismic loss of spearhead Ben King, a man who has booted 230 goals over the last four seasons. How do they replace him? Perhaps it's the incoming Aidan Schubert, but he's years away from having a real impact. Making matters worse, it seems Brownlow medallist Matt Rowell is likely to request a trade back to Victoria at the end of next season. This club is in a real precarious spot right now. A penny for Christian Petracca's thoughts...

Grade: C-

GWS Giants
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Toby Greene, Kieren Briggs, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield

2026 draft selections: 9, 20, 26, 59, 77, 86

Just two years ago Toby Greene, Kieren Briggs, Jesse Hogan, and Lachie Whitfield were probably four of the Giants' most important players. None of them remain at the club after an action-packed trade and free agency window, with GWS instead opting to clear out and trust the youth underneath. It's a move that will either make the Giants look like geniuses or total fools, but even those who are incredibly bullish about the approach would concede there is likely to be some pain on the immediate horizon.

Grade: D

Hawthorn
Incoming: Zach Merrett, Ben King, Josh Goater

Outgoing: Finn Maginness, Aidan Schubert, Sam Butler, Bodie Ryan

2026 draft selections: 29, 37, 71, 94

The Hawks should probably be the 2027 flag favourites after a whirlwind two weeks that's seen them finally land former Essendon skipper Zach Merrett, as well as Ben King. Merrett adds depth, experience, and A-grade ball use to Hawthorn's midfield group, while King provides a focal point in attack, taking the burden off the ageing Jack Gunston. Sure, Hawthorn gave up some depth, but their best 23 has improved out of sight and they still have draft collateral over the next few years to ensure talent keeps coming through the door.

Grade: A+

Melbourne
Incoming: Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, Bodie Ryan

Outgoing: Jack Viney, Trent Rivers

2026 draft selections: 4, 14, 48, 52

Just about everyone panicked when the Demons farewelled premiership heroes Christian Petracca and Clayton Oliver last year, and look how that turned out. This club seems to have a plan for the future and it isn't prepared to compromise on what it wants. Melbourne has nailed its draft picks in recent times and with selections four and 14 this year, you'd expect two more highly talented prospects to join the ranks. Who knows if Zane Duursma will work out, but they've landed him for a fraction of what the Kangaroos gave up at the draft three years ago. It's a low risk punt worth taking.

Grade: C

North Melbourne
Incoming: Nick Blakey

Outgoing: Zane Duursma, Josh Goater

2026 draft selections: 33, 49, 66, 74, 84

Credit to the Kangaroos, they finally landed a big name. The only problem is I'm not sure Nick Blakey is the superstar many are claiming. There's no doubt Blakey will add drive and dash off halfback, but is he the player you look to in the closing stages of a tight game? North also gave up a truckload of future draft capital to get him through the door which will hurt them in the coming years. And then there's the Zane Duursma fiasco. Losing a player the club invested pick No. 4 in just three years ago is an unmitigated disaster. With no selections inside the top 30 this year, it will be a rare draft without the Roos being a major player.

Grade: C+

Port Adelaide
Incoming: Luke Pedlar

Outgoing: Zak Butters

2026 draft selections: 7, 12, 22, 24, 34, 46, 65

You're never going to feel great when a player of Zak Butters' class and calibre walks out the door, but the silver lining for Port Adelaide is that Dougie Cochrane should be set to walk back in. The academy talent is the consensus best player in the upcoming draft and the Power are in a position to match any bids on their man. Expect Port to be heavily involved in the draft over the next couple of years as they look to rebuild around the likes of Cochrane, Connor Rozee, and Jason Horne-Francis.

Grade: B

Richmond
Incoming: Kieren Briggs, Nathan O'Driscoll

Outgoing: N/A

2026 draft selections: 2, 5, 44, 81

The Tigers found Toby Nankervis' successor in Kieren Briggs, who crosses from the Giants as a free agent. That's a nice win. Nathan O'Driscoll was unable to find a place in Fremantle's best team of late but should receive far more opportunity in the black and yellow jumper in 2027. Richmond has two more picks inside the top five, though they are likely to be shuffled down a few spots with bid matching on Dougie Cochrane and Cody Walker, and they simply must nail them. Even still, this side will remain incredibly young in 2027.

Grade: C

St Kilda
Incoming: Sam Marshall

Outgoing: Rowan Marshall

2026 draft selections: 10, 16, 41, 51, 69, 87

The Saints went all-in last year, signing Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Liam Ryan, and Sam Flanders. They weren't nearly as busy this off-season, and few expected them to be. Long-time ruck Rowan Marshall departs the club for the Cats, while Sam Marshall joins and should bolster their midfield stocks. Outside of that, St Kilda will be hoping to cash in with their two first round draft selections. If not, it could spell the end of Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera's tenure. This team wouldn't want to be starting 2027 slowly...

Grade: C

Sydney Swans
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Joel Amartey, Nick Blakey

2026 draft selections: 6, 38, 39, 47, 54, 76, 95

Two best 23 players departed the Swans this past fortnight with halfback Nick Blakey being traded to the Kangaroos and key forward Joel Amartey signing with the Blues as a free agent. Don't forget, Callum Mills is unlikely to suit up for the entire year after suffering an ACL injury during this year's finals campaign. That's three best 23 players to replace! Who knows what's happening with Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner? Swans fans will be praying for a hit with pick No. 6 at the upcoming draft to soften the blow.

Grade: C-

West Coast Eagles
Incoming: Jack Viney, Trent Rivers

Outgoing: N/A

2026 draft selections: 3, 23, 58, 64, 73, 82

It's clear the Eagles don't want to take the same approach as the Tigers and rely solely on the kids. Instead, they're continuing to add experienced pieces around their young talent in an effort to ease the rebuild and avoid a nosedive in morale. Jack Viney and Trent Rivers add premiership experience to the club and they haven't had to give up too much to get them. West Coast will feature prominently at November's draft with pick No. 3, 23, as well as a compensation pick in the likely scenario that the club's first selection is pushed back by a bid.

Grade: C+

Western Bulldogs
Incoming: Jordon Butts, Finn Maginness, Hudson O'Keeffe, Zak Butters

Outgoing: N/A

2026 draft selections: 42, 53, 55, 83, 89, 91

The Bulldogs now possess the most dynamic midfield trio in the game with Zak Butters joining skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards in the red, white, and blue. It's a marquee signing for Luke Beveridge's team that simply has to put them into premiership contention. Jordon Butts also joins the club and will bolster what's traditionally been a weaker defensive unit. Don't forget about key forward star Sam Darcy, who will return from a season-ending ACL injury.

Grade: A+

stories.headline: 'All love': All Blacks inspiring NZ's Rugby League World Cup tilt
stories.summary: Buoyed by a visit from their All Blacks brothers, Stacey Jones's ambitious Kiwis are out to open the rugby league World Cup with a bang by completing a memorable New Zealand double over Australia.
stories.body:
Buoyed by a visit from their All Blacks brothers, Stacey Jones's ambitious Kiwis are out to open the rugby league World Cup with a bang by completing a memorable New Zealand double over Australia.

Five days after the All Blacks crushed the Wallabies 50-19 to clinch the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd straight year, the Kiwis and Kangaroos clash in a trans-Tasman blockbuster in Sydney on Thursday night to kick off the global showpiece.

Eight ABs, including superstar winger Will Jordan and playmaker Cam Roigard, cast aside the cross-code rivalry to drop into New Zealand's captain's run on Wednesday and throw their support behind Jones's side.

"It's just all love and supporting each other and hopefully we can go watch their game on Saturday too, so it's pretty special," New Zealand captain James Fisher-Harris said.

"How dominant and how they go about their business and represent New Zealand, there's a lot of things that they do that we look up to so yeah, it's pretty cool."

Leading what he believes is "potentially" the best Kiwi forward pack ever, Fisher-Harris says "the plan" is to lift the World Cup and, like the Warriors, continue to inspire a whole new generation of rugby league players back in their homeland just like the 2008 winners did.

"When they won in 2008, I was watching Blairy (Adam Blair) and that, (Nathan) Cayless and obviously Benji (Marshall), so that made me want to go down this path," the enforcer said.

"So hopefully we can do something like that. When you are successful like that, it gets you motivated and you want to play for a certain team or a certain code.

"So that's the plan anyways, to be successful in this World Cup."

Behind the monster pack will be Kayln Ponga for the first time after the talismanic fullback, at 28, opted to represent his parents' homeland.

"He's playing pretty good right about now," Fisher-Harris said of Ponga, who led Newcastle on their magical run from seventh to a 19-18 grand final loss to the Sydney Roosters.

"But it's not just his playing ability, it's his leadership and he's been in the game for a while now.

"He's won a few things but it looks like he's pretty keen to get in that black and white jersey."

Coach Stacey Jones also believes Australia's loss is very much New Zealand's gain.

"For the Knights this year and particularly the back end of the season, he carried them to a grand final," Jones said.

"Obviously had a lot of support around him, but he's got a lot of confidence in his game at the moment and we're just lucky that we've got him on our side."

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Previews, stats, betting info for all 11 games on Thursday
stories.summary: It's another big night on the calendar for hockey fans. Here's what to watch in each contest.
stories.body:
After the overwhelming cornucopia of NHL action on Frozen Frenzy night this week, there was a brief respite with just two games on the schedule on Wednesday.

It's another loaded evening on Thursday with 22 teams in action, including some vitriolic local rivalries.

Atop that list is the first regular-season meeting of 2026-27 between the Devils and Rangers, a.k.a. the Battle of the Hudson.

Here's a look at the key stats and storylines in that game and every other contest, along with betting info and broadcast details:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Buffalo Sabres at Toronto Maple Leafs

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TOR -118, O/U: 6.5

There is a bit more distance between Buffalo and Toronto than Manhattan and Newark (around 100 miles or 160 kilometers), but these two Atlantic Division rivals have staged some epic clashes. As the Sabres look to extend a new postseason streak to two seasons, the Leafs are one of the teams challenging them for a spot. Expect some messages to be sent in this one.

New York Islanders at Ottawa Senators

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | OTT -166, O/U: 5.5

These two teams made one of the most (eventually) infamous trades of the early aughts, as Alexei Yashin was shipped to the Island on June 23, 2001 in exchange for Zdeno Chara, Bill Muckalt and the Isles' first-round pick in 2001 (No. 2 overall, used to select Jason Spezza).

As for current events, this game could feature two of the NHL's most impressive goaltenders in between the pipes at either end: Ottawa's Linus Ullmark enters the game 5-0-0, with a 1.27 goals-against average and .948 save percentage while New York's Ilya Sorokin is 3-2-0 with a 1.81 and .934, respectively.

Seattle Kraken at Tampa Bay Lightning

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TB -230, O/U: 6.5

The Lightning enter this contest on pace for 112 points this season, and are currently third in their division. No major surprise there for the perennial contenders. On the other hand, the Kraken's point pace (120) and spot in the standings (third in the Pacific) has certainly raised some eyebrows. Are they for real? This is another litmus test.

Vancouver Canucks at Florida Panthers

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | FLA -298, O/U: 6.5

During the 2024 and 2025 Stanley Cup Finals, much was made about the distance that the Panthers and Oilers had to travel between cities. If these two teams both made the Cup Final, it would be about 200 miles further in the air. Given the current state of the Canucks that seems pretty unlikely. Nevertheless, this matchup should be a fun watch, given how much both teams enjoy scoring -- and how much the Canucks seem to enjoy letting their opponents score too.

New York Rangers at New Jersey Devils

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NJ -148, O/U: 6.5

Which team will get to set the tone first in the season series? The Devils won two of three over the Rangers in 2025-26, and due to an odd scheduling quirk all four games between the clubs will take place by the end of December (Dec. 7, Dec. 15 and Dec. 22 are the others).

Both teams are led in scoring by a No. 1 draft pick -- Alexis Lafreniere (2020) has 10 points, while Jack Hughes (2019) has eight -- and both are coming off of Ws on Frozen Frenzy night.

Read more about Devils GM Sunny Mehta from Greg Wyshynski here.

Philadelphia Flyers at Detroit Red Wings

7:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+/Disney+/Hulu) | DET -135, O/U: 5.5

Neither of these teams has gotten off the blocks in a particularly strong fashion -- the Flyers are still seeking victory No. 1, while the Red Wings have just one -- but perhaps the victor here will gain some momentum. Both clubs could use some goal-suppression improvement, sitting in the bottom third of teams in goals against per game.

Kristen Shilton explores how the Red Wings are traversing through this season amid all the off-ice chaos.

Winnipeg Jets at Chicago Blackhawks

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | WPG -135, O/U: 6.5

The Blackhawks got Connor Bedard back on the ice on Tuesday -- a Frozen Frenzy miracle! -- but the Jets are still waiting for some finality in their standoff with Connor Hellebuyck. The Hellebuyck-less Jets thus head to the Windy City looking to extend their win streak, while the Blackhawks are hoping that Bedard's return sparks them to get back among the playoff contenders by season's end.

San Jose Sharks at Nashville Predators

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NSH -142, O/U: 6.5

Speaking of getting back among the playoff contenders, that sounds good to both of these teams as well -- particularly since both finished just four points back of the second wild-card spot last season. The Sharks are coming off two straight losses at home, so perhaps the slump buster comes on the road. Steven Stamkos leads the way thus far for Nashville with seven points (three goals, four assists) through six games.

St. Louis Blues at Minnesota Wild

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | MIN -155, O/U: 6.5

Much has changed since these two clubs were the Western wild cards in 2024-25 (and finished separated by just a point in the standings). Minnesota has leveled up to the top echelon of Western powers, while St. Louis is looking for the kind of consistency that'll get it back in the perennial postseason mix. The Blues took two of three games against the Wild last season despite the standings disparity; who will earn the first W of the four-game series this time around?

Utah Mammoth at Edmonton Oilers

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | EDM -142, O/U: 6.5

It's no surprise that the Oilers are among the leading teams in the Western standings this season; no team that includes two perennial Hart Trophy candidates in Connor McDavid and Leon Draisaitl should drift far from contention. What is at least a little surprising outside the 801 area code is that the Mammoth are your current Central Division leaders after two weeks and change.

This will be an excellent early test for Clayton Keller, Nick Schmaltz & Co. to show that they belong in the contention conversation for the long haul.

Calgary Flames at Vegas Golden Knights

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | VGK -290, O/U: 6.5

The rebuilding Flames have thus far performed about on par with expectations: through six games, they're 31st in the NHL in scoring (only the Flyers have scored fewer than their 2.00 goals per game), and 32nd in goals against per game, at 4.83. They'll pay a visit to the Pacific-leading Golden Knights -- and the sportsbooks don't give them much of a chance. But maybe they'll pull out another shocking W, as they did as underdogs against the Ducks on Tuesday.

Reminder: Fans can catch all the action in the NHL streaming hub and on the ESPN App.
