stories.headline: 15 NFL players, coaches on the hot seat entering Week 6: Quinn, McDaniel, others
stories.summary: What now for Mike McDaniel? Should the Commanders or Eagles consider coaching changes? Could Jacoby Brissett or Brian Thomas Jr. get traded?
stories.body:
Week 6 is about the point where seats start getting hot around the NFL. Five games isn't a huge sample for coaches and players, but it's enough time to see with some confidence that preseason expectations or hopes aren't going to be met. It's enough time for fans to be frustrated and make their feelings known in stadiums and on social media.

Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show'

There's no joy in seeing anyone around the league lose their job or miss out on an opportunity, but it's also a reality that everybody who works for a team faces on an annual basis. Today, I'm going to run through some of the players and coaches on the proverbial hot seat after the first five weeks of the 2026 NFL season and break down what's going wrong and what might happen next.

In no particular order, I'll hit on three head coaches, two coordinators and 10 players with questions about their futures with their current teams. And I'll begin with a coordinator for a winless team that entered the season with postseason aspirations.

Jump to a player or coach:

McDaniel | Montgomery | Bland | Smack

Bowles | Quinn | Sainristil | Sirianni

Sheppard | Hairston | Jeudy | Brissett

Smith | Thomas | Nix

Mike McDaniel, OC, Los Angeles Chargers
It seems natural to talk about what must be the most disappointing unit in football this season. And it's fair to note that, yet again, injuries have waylaid the Chargers on the offensive side of the ball. In last week's 23-17 loss to the Broncos, the Chargers were down their top two wide receivers (Quentin Johnston and Ladd McConkey, the latter of whom was active but did not play a single snap) and their three best offensive linemen (Joe Alt, Tyler Biadasz and Rashawn Slater). Justin Herbert's lone touchdown pass went to Hayden Rucci, a tight end who was signed off Jacksonville's practice squad in mid-September.

Even so, McDaniel's old employers in San Francisco have had plenty of injuries on offense and things are still humming along just fine for the 49ers. Frankly, even before the injuries really slowed this offense down, things didn't look the way they were supposed to in Los Angeles. The Chargers haven't been able to run the ball all season, ranking 28th in EPA per play on designed rushes.

McDaniel has been insistent on running into heavy boxes with limited success; the Chargers have faced a numbers disadvantage in the run game 36.2% of the time per NFL Next Gen Stats, which is the fifth-worst rate in the league. It's fine to run into loaded boxes if you trust your linemen to pull it off, but the Chargers are averaging 2.5 yards per carry and minus-0.32 EPA per play on those attempts while picking up first downs at the fifth-lowest rate in the NFL.

What has to be more concerning for coach Jim Harbaugh, though, is the regression of Herbert. Through five weeks, Herbert is last among qualifying passers in Total QBR (26.6). By several notable metrics, Herbert has completely collapsed as a passer:

Herbert's sack rate is up, and he leads the league in interceptions with seven. And while a couple of those have been the customary snaps where a Chargers receiver is suddenly allergic to the football at the point of arrival and coughs it up to a defender, Herbert deserves plenty of blame for the problems the Chargers have had as games wear on. He has a 5.0 QBR in the fourth quarter, throwing four picks and taking a league-high five strip sacks. His fourth-down interception against the Broncos last week was one of the worst throws you'll ever see Herbert make, a lowlight he seems adamant about challenging every week once the Chargers get behind late in games.

There's usually not much benefit to making an in-season change at offensive coordinator, given that the positional coaches were likely brought in by that coordinator and would just be running the same scheme if they were promoted to the playcalling role. The most experienced assistant on McDaniel's staff is passing game specialist Adam Gase, which won't inspire much hope among Chargers fans.

They do have Harbaugh, though, and there's a clear line that the offensive coordinator in Los Angeles can't cross. It's one thing to field a disappointing run game or fail to live up to expectations, but the offense can't break Herbert. If McDaniel can't turn things around, and Herbert continues to struggle badly, the Chargers might make a move sooner rather than later.

David Montgomery, RB, Houston Texans
The latest in a series of offseason additions to try to fix a moribund Texans running game, Montgomery hasn't been able to transfer his successful three-year stretch in Detroit to Houston. Though the 2019 third-round pick scored three touchdowns in the Week 1 loss to the Bills, Montgomery has averaged just 2.7 yards per carry and posted a league-worst 23.1% success rate. You can help compensate for those issues with explosive runs, but Montgomery has just one gain of 10-plus yards across 52 carries this season.

Montgomery left last week's win over the Titans in the first half with a groin injury, potentially opening up the door to a larger role for Woody Marks. The second-year pro had what qualifies as a great game on the ground for a Texans back, turning 15 carries into 62 yards while adding four catches for 23 yards as a receiver. The Texans have been hesitant to turn the lead role over to Marks, but Montgomery's struggles and the groin injury might leave them no choice.

DaRon Bland, CB, Dallas Cowboys
Bland was a first-team All-Pro after he picked off nine passes in 2023, but the interceptions have dried up since then. He has just one INT across 24 games since the start of 2024. And when Bland isn't creating significant value with his takeaways, teams find it too easy to pick on him in coverage. He has allowed passer ratings north of 100 in coverage in each of the past three seasons, per Pro-Football-Reference.com, including a career-worst 126.2 mark this season.

Jerry Jones and the Cowboys have had reasons to give Bland a long leash. Despite missing most of the 2024 season with a foot injury, the Cowboys gave their young corner a four-year, $90 million extension before the 2025 season. Bland missed more time last year before pronouncing himself to be all the way back this season ... but he has looked overmatched in coverage. Tez Johnson's 64-yard catch against the Cowboys in primetime last week came on a play where Bland was badly juked and fell to the ground like he was the child in one of those "dad crosses over baby" videos.

The Cowboys didn't really have solutions to replace Bland on the outside at cornerback, but that has changed. Cobie Durant should be set to return from his hamstring injury in the coming weeks, while Joey Porter Jr. will be back in the lineup after missing the loss to the Buccaneers with an illness. When healthy, they should be the starters on the outside for Dallas. Bland could end up in the slot, but the Cowboys have been playing Reddy Steward there, and rookie safety Caleb Downs could move there once Jalen Thompson returns from his hamstring injury.

Dallas restructured Bland's deal just before the season, which reduced his cap hit and made his contract more tradable. But it also creates more dead money if (or more realistically when) the Cowboys decide to move on from the 27-year-old cornerback. Bland is owed $13 million next year, and at the moment, it's only guaranteed for injury. The Cowboys don't want to be on the hook for that money, so it would hardly be a surprise if they took Bland out of the lineup altogether once Durant and Porter are back on the field to avoid triggering those guarantees, which would happen if Bland suffers a significant injury.

Trey Smack, K, Green Bay Packers
Life is tough for rookie kickers. Coaches don't trust you. Fans want an excuse to turn on you. You might get only a handful of kicks to prove that you're an NFL-caliber player. The leash is a little longer if you're a draftee, but competitive teams just don't have much patience with unproven kickers once the season actually begins and games are on the line.

As a sixth-round pick, Smack was clearly prioritized by the Packers as the replacement for Brandon McManus, who might have cost Green Bay its wild-card game with the Bears after missing two field goals and an extra point. And before Sunday, Smack was having a reasonable start to his pro career, having missed just one field goal and one extra point through four games.

In a blowout victory over those same Bears, though, Smack struggled badly. He missed an extra point and field goal attempts from 43 and 47 yards out, matching McManus' performance in the wild-card loss. All three kicks were wide. And though the Packers have to deal with the reality that it's hard to kick in wintry conditions once the calendar hits December and January in Green Bay, this game was played on a 73-degree day with modest wind.

One bad game shouldn't sink Smack. If he struggles in the weeks to come, though, the Packers might not be willing to go into the winter with an inexperienced kicker, especially given what happened to them in the postseason a year ago.

Todd Bowles, HC, Tampa Bay Buccaneers
One win against the Cowboys slowed the criticism of Bowles, whose Bucs had gotten off to an 0-4 start before turning things around against Dallas. The victory ended a stretch where the Buccaneers had gone 2-11 since their bye in 2025, including the first four games of the 2026 season. That run cost them what appeared to be a procession to the NFC South title in 2025 and put them behind the eight ball to start 2026.

With rookie Jalon Daniels in at quarterback for the injured Baker Mayfield, Bowles will have to hope his defense can carry the Bucs in the weeks to come against the likes of the Panthers, Falcons and Bears. Bowles' defense was primarily responsible for the collapse after the bye in 2025, ranking 26th in points allowed per drive and 28th in defensive EPA per snap over that span.

Things have been better on that side of the ball to start the year in 2026. Tampa is fourth in EPA allowed per play and ninth in points allowed per drive. The Buccaneers are somehow doing that with a formula that doesn't make sense. Bowles' defense is blitzing at the fourth-highest rate in the league, but the Bucs rank only 28th in sack rate. Instead, they are winning by stopping the run at the fifth-best rate in the NFL by success rate and getting off the field on third down, where they have the eighth-best defensive stop rate.

Bowles started his second head coaching stint by making three straight playoff appearances, including a blowout victory over the Eagles in 2023. That success bought Bowles some slack. It's also clear that the second-half collapse took a toll on the organization, leading Bowles to fire five assistants after the season. That's usually the last move before a head coach follows his former assistants out the door. If Bowles can stick in the NFC South race and stay afloat until Mayfield returns, he should be back in 2027. If Tampa goes on another losing streak, though, Bowles might have to walk the plank.

Dan Quinn, HC, Washington Commanders
Well, you saw the end of that Giants-Commanders game. While I pin some of the blame for what went wrong on Jayden Daniels and David Blough, as the head coach, Quinn is the one most responsible for making sure his young QB and offensive coordinator know what to do in those situations. Given that Quinn has handed over the defense to Daronte Jones, the 56-year-old should be even more focused on the sort of game management issues that cost the Commanders a shot at a victory Sunday.

Since Quinn stunningly led the Commanders to a 12-5 season and a trip to the NFC Championship Game in his debut year with the organization, things have quickly gone south. Injuries to Daniels sank the team's chances in 2025, but Quinn was blamed for leaving Daniels in the game when he suffered an elbow injury; Washington was trailing by 31 points in the fourth quarter of a loss to the Seahawks.

Washington's defense also collapsed in 2025, finishing 30th in points allowed per drive, leading Quinn to fire defensive coordinator Joe Whitt Jr. The organization invested heavily in free agency to shore up the unit this offseason and hired Jones to take over the defense, but the early results haven't been much better, as the Commanders are up to only 26th in points allowed per possession. They blew a 14-point lead to the Giants on Sunday and couldn't stop Jameis Winston from moving the ball in overtime, with the defense bailed out by a missed field goal and a Cam Skattebo fumble.

Quinn's team is now 3-13-1 over its past 17 games, with one of those victories coming against the Eagles backups in Week 18. Any attempt to draw a line under 2025 as an aberration hasn't been successful, given that the defense has continued to struggle and Daniels has already suffered another elbow injury in 2026. I thought calls to fire Quinn for the endgame on Sunday were too harsh, but there's no denying that this is the sort of disaster that lingers in fans' minds.

If Quinn can't turn things around, there's the risk of this becoming the sort of tenure-defining collapse that Quinn was on the other side of when the Hail Mary past Tyrique Stevenson Sr. in 2024 was the beginning of the end for Matt Eberflus in Chicago.

Mike Sainristil, CB, Washington Commanders
Just as Quinn excelled in 2024 and hasn't seemed like the same difference-maker since then, Sainristil has also struggled to live up to his first year in Washington. A second-round pick who was expected to be a high-end slot cornerback, Sainristil quickly emerged as an option on the outside for the Commanders, finishing ninth in Defensive Rookie of the Year balloting. He then picked off two passes in the postseason, leading to hope that Sainristil could be a young cornerstone for the Commanders.

Instead, he has gone backward. He was one of the many Commanders who struggled last season, allowing a passer rating north of 100 despite intercepting four passes. This year, Sainristil looked even worse in the Week 1 defeat against the Eagles, losing a deep ball in the air to Dontayvion Wicks for Philadelphia's biggest play of the day. He has allowed a 147.6 passer rating in coverage.

Quinn already made his move in Week 3, benching Sainristil after two frustrating starts in favor of veteran journeyman Rasul Douglas. Sainristil ran ahead of Fabian Moreau as the team's nickel cornerback Sunday, playing 48% of the defensive snaps, but the Commanders are about to get 2025 second-round pick Trey Amos back from a fractured fibula. Sainristil will need to play well when he does get on the field to have a shot at winning his job back.

Nick Sirianni, HC, Philadelphia Eagles
Though its impact was muted by its timing in London and the Commanders fiasco that ensued later on Sunday, Sirianni didn't cover himself in glory at the end of Sunday's frustrating loss to the Jaguars. While the Eagles understandably wanted extra yardage to make Jake Elliott's field goal to take the lead easier, Sirianni saw rookie wide receiver Makai Lemon step out of bounds after making a catch, stopping the clock for the Jaguars. And after taking the lead, Sirianni elected to kick the ball into the field of play, with the ensuing return setting the Jags up for a last-second field goal to steal the game away.

Sirianni's decision wasn't quite as cut-and-dried as it might seem. For one, the Eagles might have been just as likely to allow one big completion after a touchback as they were to give up the kickoff return that got Jacksonville in field goal range. If this were one isolated endgame scenario for an otherwise successful organization, the hot seat for Sirianni wouldn't extend outside of Philadelphia sports radio.

Of course, the Eagles have been frustrating for quite a while now. The offense wasn't at its best in 2025, with Philly going 3-4 down the stretch before losing in the wild-card round at home to the 49ers. The Eagles dramatically changed things during the offseason, firing coordinator Kevin Patullo and moving on from legendary offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland. They hired Sean Mannion as the new OC to reimagine the offense by going under center more often and relying on a zone-rushing attack.

Those moves haven't worked. The Eagles are 30th in EPA per play on offense, down from 17th a year ago. Injuries to Saquon Barkley, DeVonta Smith and multiple offensive linemen (and the non-injury-related departures of Cam Jurgens and Lane Johnson) haven't helped, of course, but there really hasn't been a sustained stretch all season where the offense has looked explosive, regardless of who was on the field.

And as I wrote about last year, Sirianni's lack of clear ownership over any one particular piece of the operation makes him more likely to receive blame for what goes wrong than credit for what goes right. Sirianni's résumé through five-plus years as Eagles head coach is as good as anybody's in NFL history, but for various reasons, there's a clear perception that Sirianni isn't the one driving much of that success.

And while Sirianni has racked up a gaudy win-loss record during his time in Philadelphia, the Eagles are 5-7 over their past 12 games, including a three-game losing streak. Three of their next four games are at home against the Panthers, Cowboys and Giants, all games we would expect Sirianni's team to win. If the Eagles win games, even in ugly fashion, fans will tolerate the struggles. But if the losing streak continues, well, the sudden end to Doug Pederson's tenure with the team in 2020 should tell you just how quickly an otherwise successful run can come to a sudden close in Philadelphia.

Kelvin Sheppard, DC, Detroit Lions
When the Lions lost coordinators Ben Johnson and Aaron Glenn after the 2024 season to head coaching gigs, Dan Campbell chose a pair of relatively low-key replacements. He hired John Morton from the Broncos to take over the offense and promoted Sheppard, already on staff as the team's linebackers coach, to run the defense. Given how successful Campbell's prior hires had been, the new coordinators deservedly started their tenure with some credit in the bank.

That credit is all used up. Morton didn't make it through one full year as offensive playcaller. Campbell took over the role during the 2025 season before firing Morton after missing the playoffs. Sheppard made it through Year 1, but unless things improve, it's tough to see him surviving through the end of a second season in the defensive role. The Lions are a disaster on defense, ranking 29th in points allowed per drive and last in EPA per play. They can't get off the field on third down and have allowed teams to convert 81% of their red zone trips into touchdowns, the third-worst figure in the league.

Is that on coaching? I'm skeptical. Watching the Lions closely, I see a defense that simply doesn't have enough talent as opposed to one that makes routine schematic mistakes. The Lions comfortably have the worst secondary in the NFL, a product of injuries (which have cost them one of the league's best safety duos in Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph) and off-field behavior (leading to the release of 2024 first-round pick Terrion Arnold, who admittedly wasn't living up to expectations before being cut amid felony charges of armed robbery and kidnapping).

Longtime starter D.J. Reed hasn't played well, but the players around him shouldn't be expected to make up a solid secondary. Sheppard is running out veterans on low-cost contracts such as Chuck Clark, Roger McCreary, Rock Ya-Sin and Christian Izien as regular defensive backs. Players such as Thomas Harper and Avonte Maddox weren't playing well, either, but they've also gone down injured, leaving the Lions without alternatives. It's telling that Detroit was excited to turn to rookie Keith Abney II, a 5-foot-9 fifth-round pick, as a potential savior at corner against the Cardinals last week. It's difficult to recall a secondary that was less imposing on paper, let alone how it has played in reality.

The good news for the Lions, if there is any, is that the front four is playing better. The Lions have the fifth-best sack rate in the league. They're the second-best tackling team in terms of missed tackle rate, although that doesn't cover situations where the Lions simply aren't close enough to a ball carrier to even attempt a tackle. If the Lions could hold up in coverage, the defense might improve to passable, which would be enough to win plenty of games given the way the offense is playing.

One major reinforcement is on the way in Branch, who has returned to practice and should be back on the field in the next couple of weeks from his Achilles injury. Abney had a solid start against the Cardinals and should feature in the defense more often moving forward. And though Joseph's future is unclear after suffering a knee injury last year, the hope is that the Lions will have the 2024 first-team All-Pro back at some point in 2026.

If Abney and Branch can't right the ship, something will need to change. General manager Brad Holmes is aggressive and could look to make a move at the trade deadline, with Campbell admitting that the Lions were in on the Joey Porter Jr. negotiations before the Cowboys swooped in and traded for the Steelers corner. Sheppard will obviously hope to get more help, but the Lions can't compete for a title if their defense continues to blow leads in the fourth quarter.

Maxwell Hairston, CB, Buffalo Bills
The reckoning might have already come for Hairston, Buffalo's first-round pick in the 2025 draft. His rookie year was compromised by a knee injury that cost him the first six games of the campaign. He ended up starting just three games all season and then missed the two postseason games that ended Sean McDermott's tenure with an ankle injury.

This season was supposed to be a fresh start for Hairston, but his first month was a mess. The 23-year-old allowed two touchdown passes in the 29-26 loss to the Patriots, leading defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard to publicly encourage Hairston to temper his emotions. Hairston also left the locker room after the defeat without speaking to the media before returning and apologizing a day later.

The Bills have said the right thing publicly, but actions speak louder than words. Against the Rams on Monday, Hairston's snap share cratered with the return of Christian Benford. The Bills kept Davison Igbinosun in the lineup ahead of Hairston, who played just 15 snaps on defense. Igbinosun committed a pass interference penalty in the red zone and allowed a touchdown catch, which won't help his case, but he still appears to be ahead of Hairston on the depth chart.

Jerry Jeudy, WR, Cleveland Browns
The Browns are excited about their young wide receiver duo of Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion, although Concepcion was forced out of last week's loss to the Jets with a concussion. Harold Fannin Jr. is a building block at tight end, too. There's less chatter about Jeudy, whose role in the offense has been inconsistent. Jeudy saw steady snaps last week after Concepcion's injury, but he had been playing about half of the offensive snaps on a weekly basis beforehand, dropping down to 38% in the Week 4 win over the Steelers.

Jeudy has a line of eight catches for 81 yards this season, but he's still only 27 years old and two years removed from a 1,229-yard campaign for the Browns in 2024. It's tough to see a long-term future for him in Cleveland, but how he plays over the next few weeks might determine whether there's real interest at the trade deadline from a team that wants to give the 2020 first-round pick a meaningful role. If not, Jeudy might lose snaps to Boston, Concepcion, Isaiah Bond and tight ends in the second half of the year.

Jacoby Brissett, QB, Arizona Cardinals
I have been an avowed Brissett fan for years given his incredibly low interception rate and ability to at least competently sustain just about any offense in football. Through five games in 2026, though, Brissett is averaging just 5.6 yards per attempt and has thrown five picks. One of those was a Hail Mary against the Lions last week, but Brissett threw three interceptions in the previous week's loss to the Giants, including a pick-six on the final snap of the game to Deonte Banks.

Brissett's ability to pick up first downs on sneaks and complete a high percentage of his passes appeals to Total QBR, which has him 16th among all quarterbacks through five games. But with Brissett 30th in yards per dropback and the Cardinals last by a considerable margin in explosive play rate (5.5%) on offense, this is a case where I think my own feelings and those of the organization might disagree with QBR.

The Cardinals aren't particularly motivated to win games this season given the likelihood that they'll draft a quarterback in 2026. They're also likely interested in seeing what they have in third-round pick Carson Beck, who posted a 125.4 passer rating in the preseason. If there's a trade market for Brissett at the deadline, the Cardinals might consider just moving forward with Beck and Gardner Minshew II as their two options under center. And if not, Brissett might be sitting behind the rookie by the time we get to November anyway.

Genesis Smith, S, Los Angeles Chargers
It's tough to be a rookie on a collapsing team that's drastically coming up short of expectations, and Smith isn't the biggest problem in Los Angeles. And the fourth-round pick did come up with two interceptions of Josh Allen in Week 3. But Smith has otherwise struggled in coverage, having a particularly rough day against the Raiders in Week 2. He also appeared to be at fault on the lone touchdown pass of the day for the Broncos on Sunday, flying into the flat to take a covered receiver while letting Courtland Sutton run past him for an easy score.

The Chargers haven't had star safety Derwin James Jr. on the field for the past couple of games, but the five-time Pro Bowler should be back in the lineup after recovering from a hamstring injury. Jim Harbaugh could choose to treat the rest of the year as a lost cause and stick with his young guys to get them reps, but I wouldn't be shocked if the Chargers tried to get their most reliable players on the field and stuck with veterans James, Tony Jefferson and Elijah Molden as their three safeties when they're all healthy.

Brian Thomas Jr., WR, Jacksonville Jaguars
Though the Jaguars keep winning, Thomas' role in the offense continues to shrink. After a disappointing 2025 season was chalked up to an ankle issue that made it painful for him to run, hopes were high that he would be able to get back to his rookie-year level of production in a second season under Liam Coen in 2026.

So far, Thomas has nine catches for 105 yards through five games, including a doughnut in Sunday's win over the Eagles. (He did nearly catch a touchdown, only to narrowly step out of bounds.) The coaching staff also doesn't seem particularly desperate to get the 2024 first-round pick on the field, with Thomas playing just 48.2% of the offensive snaps. In recent weeks, the Jaguars have preferred rookie sixth-round pick Josh Cameron to Thomas for his blocking and big-play ability, particularly when they get into larger personnel groupings.

The Jaguars are committed to Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers as their top two wideouts and want to play with Brenton Strange and Nate Boerkircher on the field, which leaves a limited role for Thomas. Trading Thomas would also open up more opportunities for Travis Hunter, who has played just 21 offensive snaps while starring on defense. The organization has repeatedly insisted that it has no interest in trading Thomas, but at some point, having a valuable young player wasting away on your bench can't be the best thing for the player or the team.

Bo Nix, QB, Denver Broncos
Let's frame this one appropriately and be clear. I don't think the Broncos are about to bench Nix for backup Jarrett Stidham, who hasn't been particularly impressive as a pro and didn't play well in last season's AFC title game loss to the Patriots while filling in for the injured starter. The hot seat here is more in the big picture, with Nix becoming eligible for a contract extension after the season and a decision on his fifth-year option in 2028 (at a projected $29.9 million) coming due next spring.

Whether it has been a product of Nix recovering from the ankle injury that ended his 2025 season, not feeling right in Davis Webb's version of the offense or simply being too antsy about where to go with the football, he hasn't been an effective quarterback through five games in 2026. Nix's 41.5 Total QBR is 24th in the league. He's averaging just 5.8 yards per attempt, and only 27.8% of his throws are producing first downs, the fourth-worst rate in the league.

In years past, Nix has produced a relatively high floor by avoiding mistakes and creating plays with his legs, generating first downs for an offense that wasn't getting them through the air. Nix's interception rate and sack rate are still much better than league average, but he's generating just 7 rushing yards and 1.2 first downs per game as a runner, down from 23 rush yards and two first downs per game over the prior two seasons.

Throughout his career, Nix has been an erratic quarterback given his propensity to throw off-platform and on the move. He has a strong arm, but getting the most out of that arm requires Nix to set his feet and throw with a solid base, and all of his movement makes it difficult to actually access his arm strength. When he's playing well, Nix is an accurate passer. When he's not, the ball is all over the place, and Nix can struggle with just getting the ball out before routes have even developed.

Expectations for the offense were high after Nix's performance in the divisional round win over the Bills and the offseason acquisition of Jaylen Waddle, who gave the Broncos a much-needed threat at all three levels across from Courtland Sutton. As the Broncos struggled through the first month of the season, frustration for Denver's slow start on offense naturally fell on Webb, the 31-year-old former quarterback who had taken over playcalling duties from Sean Payton to start the season.

It wasn't much of a surprise when Payton reclaimed playcalling responsibilities before last Sunday's game over the Chargers. Yet Nix might have looked worse in Payton's first game back at the helm against what has been one of the league's most unimposing defenses. Nix went 16-of-27 for just 123 yards, and the Broncos converted only one third down in 12 tries. All 20 of their points came on drives that started on Los Angeles' side of the field.

The Broncos have more insight into the status of Nix's ankle than we do, and it's possible that the 26-year-old is playing through pain. Even if we take a step back and look at his full career, though, Nix is 19th in Total QBR since entering the league. He's 22nd in yards per dropback and 29th in yards per attempt and first-down rate. And Nix has done that with one of the league's best offensive lines and an elite architect designing the offense and calling plays.

The Broncos were hoping Nix would take a step forward after his great performance in the postseason and the addition of Waddle. If Nix doesn't get there, will the Broncos want to commit to him as their quarterback of the future on a second contract?

stories.headline: What is real -- and what isn't -- about 2026 MLB playoffs so far
stories.summary: Here's what has stood out so far this postseason -- and whether it will continue.
stories.body:
The theme of the 2026 playoffs: unhittable fastballs, unhittable changeups, unhittable sliders and sweepers and cutters and knuckle-curveballs and split-fingered fastballs. Pitchers are dominating this October like we haven't seen in decades, with batters hitting just .227 and on pace for the lowest OPS since the 1983 postseason.

Of the 30 games played, a team has scored two runs or fewer 19 times -- or 31% of all team games played. Every lead change, and there haven't been many of them, feels like a little miracle. The close, mostly low-scoring games have created a tense postseason but not necessarily the most exciting one (and last year's playoffs are a tough act to follow anyway).

While we're still in the early stages of the league championship series -- about halfway through the postseason -- let's take stock of what has happened so far, looking at the teams still alive and some of those that have been eliminated.

Teams that are still in it

The Milwaukee Brewers look unbeatable thanks to their bullpen

Verdict: Real

Milwaukee's bullpen had allowed three earned runs in 32⅔ innings, surrendering a batting average of .139. The bullpen outdueled San Diego's vaunted pen in the NLDS. It has also twice rescued Jacob Misiorowski, who didn't last five innings in either of his postseason starts. It pitched 4⅔ scoreless innings in Game 1 of the NLCS and then finished Game 2 with five perfect innings. Manager Pat Murphy has used seven different relievers, but two have stood out:

• Abner Uribe throws a 99-mph sinker and an 88-mph slider. They look like the same pitch nearing home plate, but then the sinker often dives in on right-handed batters and the slider darts away. Pick your poison. Both pitches induce a high rate of ground balls. He's often brought in to face the toughest part of an opponent's lineup. He pitched a scoreless sixth inning against the Dodgers in Game 1 and got four outs in Game 2, though he did give up two runs and walked three in Game 3.

• Aaron Ashby is a former starter who didn't pitch in the majors in 2023 because of shoulder surgery but eventually returned as a top reliever the past two seasons. The lefty's fastball averages 97.7 mph, and he has a starter's repertoire with four different pitches. He's Murphy's secret weapon of sorts, as his background means he can comfortably go multiple innings -- he was second among relievers in innings pitched in the regular season. He had a three-inning outing against the San Diego Padres and then got 11 outs in the first two games of the NLCS, earning the save in Game 2.

The Brewers have constructed elite bullpens for years now, and the common denominator for 2026: Throw hard. Their relievers have averaged 98 mph with their fastballs in the postseason (they were fourth in the regular season, averaging 95.9 mph).

Two notes here. Across the entire postseason landscape, including starting pitchers, the average fastball has clocked in at 96.1 mph, continuing the increases we've seen since pitch tracking began in 2008. And those fastballs have been harder than ever to do damage on:

The second note is that a hot bullpen has become a vital ingredient to winning in the playoffs this decade. The results for Milwaukee's bullpen so far are reminiscent of the Houston Astros' dominant postseason performance in 2022, when their relievers posted a 0.83 ERA in 54⅓ innings, allowing a .126 average. Atlanta's bullpen got hot in 2021 (closer Will Smith, after a shaky regular season, tossed 11 scoreless innings with six saves) and the Dodgers' pen carried the team to the 2024 title when its rotation was shaky.

This is a significant change from the end of the 2010s, when deep rotations created the path to championships. When the Chicago Cubs won Game 7 in 2016, then-manager Joe Maddon was determined to use just three pitchers, including starter Jon Lester in relief; only when the game went into the 10th inning did Maddon use his second and third relief pitchers. In 2017, Houston skipper A.J. Hinch dumped closer Ken Giles and used starting pitchers in relief (Charlie Morton pitched the final four innings of Game 7 of the World Series). In 2018, Boston Red Sox manager Alex Cora had five different pitchers who both started and relieved in a game. The 2019 Washington Nationals were 29th in the majors in bullpen ERA but won behind Stephen Strasburg, Max Scherzer and Patrick Corbin (who pitched three innings in relief in Game 7 of the World Series).

This year's Brewers showcase what a dominant bullpen can do: Misiorowski and Logan Henderson, their top two starters, have lasted just 17⅓ innings in their four starts, but the Brewers won all four games.

The Los Angeles Dodgers' dynasty is teetering

Verdict: Not real

Please, let's not go there just yet, even if they do have their backs against the wall in their quest to become the first NL team to win three consecutive World Series. If anything, the early results of this NLCS have shown how difficult it is to win in the postseason and to do it three years in a row -- and, really, how fortunate the Dodgers were to win the past two World Series.

Think of some of what went right for Los Angeles over the past two postseasons: shutting out the Padres for two straight games to win the 2024 NLDS, with the Mets upsetting the Phillies in the other series so the Dodgers faced an easier opponent in the NLCS; beating the Phillies last year on a pitcher throwing error; and Will Klein's Herculean, out-of-nowhere relief outing in the 2026 World Series, not to mention Miguel Rojas' unlikely home run and Isiah Kiner-Falefa not getting a bigger lead off third base.

Last year, the Dodgers' slow play of their rotation worked perfectly: Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow were all healthy and rolling in October alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto. This year, Ohtani can't pitch and Snell and Glasnow scuffled in their NLDS starts.

Ohtani's injury and offensive struggles also highlight how the Dodgers have been hemorrhaging 25 runs or so a year on offense since 2023: from 906 runs to 842 to 825 to 801. They can no longer count on superstar-level production from Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts (who, by the way, is on a 30-game homerless streak in the postseason). That average postseason fastball velocity of 96.1 mph that we mentioned? The Dodgers were 11th in the regular season in OPS against fastballs of 96-plus mph. A power staff, such as the one Milwaukee possesses, is the way to beat the Dodgers.

Of course, the Dodgers still won 100 games this season. They also have Josue De Paula, who looks like Juan Soto-Lite at the plate with his elite plate discipline and is ready to join the lineup in 2027, although they'll have to figure out how to squeeze him into the outfield with Teoscar Hernandez and Kyle Tucker still under contract. And it wouldn't be a surprise if the Dodgers find a way to sign Tarik Skubal, even with the uncertainty over the labor situation.

The organization remains strong, and it has a highly-regarded farm system beyond De Paula. But after three losses of the NLCS, the Dodgers look older and more vulnerable than at any point this decade.

Chase DeLauter is the breakout star of this postseason

Verdict: Real

DeLauter's rookie season flew under the radar, but the 2022 first-round pick hit .287/.363/.457 with 16 home runs in 133 games. He's hitting .346/.452/.538 with a home run, two doubles and four RBIs in seven games for the Cleveland Guardians in the postseason.

But here's the stat that stands out -- five walks and one strikeout. He has had some veteran at-bats: two seven-pitch walks against Freddy Peralta in Game 2, an RBI double off Ian Seymour in a left-on-left matchup later in that game, a first-pitch home run to the opposite field off Drew Rasmussen in Game 1 and a first-pitch double off Tyler Wells in the eighth inning to set up Nathaniel Lowe's two-run single that broke up a 2-2 tie.

Those types of at-bats mirror what we saw in the regular season, when DeLauter ranked in the 95th percentile in chase rate and 93rd percentile in whiff rate. He hit .323 against lefties, so that's another positive, and he should learn to tap into more power in upcoming seasons.

His issue has been staying healthy -- he played just 57 games in the minors in 2023, 39 in 2024 and 42 in 2025, so he's played more games this year than the past three combined. With fellow rookie Travis Bazzana, who had a solid season with a .245/.335/.408 line, the Guardians have added two impact bats who should be in the middle of their order for years to come.

The Tampa Bay Rays' bullpen might be more vulnerable than we thought

Verdict: Real

Nobody is doubting closer Bryan Baker. He's the reason the Rays were the only team to not lose a game it led going into the ninth inning all season. He has made four postseason appearances and hasn't allowed a hit. Manager Kevin Cash hasn't had to extend him more than three outs yet, but it's safe to say the Rays will win if they're ahead in the ninth inning.

But there have been a couple of hiccups from the rest of the bullpen in the first two games against Cleveland. The non-Baker relievers allowed five runs over the final two innings of Game 1. Wells, pitching for the first time in a month, entered in that tie game and gave up a weakly hit infield single to Jose Ramirez and then the hard-hit double to DeLauter.

Cam Booser had already pitched, so Cash turned to Seymour, his No. 2 lefty, but he allowed the go-ahead hit to Lowe (who had gone 5-for-45 against left-handers in the regular season). Seymour had spent much of the season as a starter or bulk reliever, so he rarely pitched with inherited runners -- only 10 all season. Down 4-3 in the ninth, Cash then somewhat curiously avoided Kevin Kelly, his No. 2 righty behind Baker, and instead used Cole Sulser, who allowed three runs.

The Rays won Game 2, but Seymour let another inherited runner score when DeLauter doubled off him. With Griffin Jax, who rarely goes more than five innings, and then Nick Martinez, who got pulled in the fourth inning of his ALDS start against the New York Yankees, taking the mound for Tampa Bay in Games 3 and 4, Cash might not get a lot of length from his starters these next two games. Whether the Rays can get the ball to Baker with the lead now looks like the biggest question of this series.

Teams that have been eliminated

The Philadelphia Phillies will look vastly different when we see them next

Verdict: Not real

We asked this same question a year ago after the Phillies lost to the Dodgers in the NLDS and many suggested the Phillies needed a makeover. Following their wild-card series loss to the Atlanta Braves this year, we came up with the same answer: not real. That proved mostly correct as the Phillies re-signed free agents Kyle Schwarber and J.T. Realmuto this past offseason, although they did lose Ranger Suarez to the Red Sox. The core offensive group of Schwarber, Realmuto, Bryce Harper, Bryson Stott, Brandon Marsh and Alec Bohm have all been here for the team's five postseason appearances since 2022, with Trea Turner joining in 2023, a remarkable run of lineup uniformity.

The Phillies are mostly stuck with this aging group at this point. Bohm is a free agent, so he's probably gone, with rookie Aidan Miller a good bet to take over at shortstop or third base -- Turner's defensive metrics were terrible, so it might be time to move him to another position, perhaps the outfield. Stott and Marsh are heading into their free agent seasons, so they could be trade bait, but neither will return much. Indeed, that's kind of the problem here: The position player group was remarkably healthy in 2026, with seven players appearing in at least 149 games (six with at least 155) and catcher Realmuto playing in 123, yet those eight players were worth just a combined 7.4 WAR via Baseball-Reference. Marsh (0.4), Realmuto (0.0), Turner (minus-0.1), Bohm (minus-0.2) and Justin Crawford (minus-0.2) were essentially replacement level players.

That's why the Phillies didn't win the division despite the stellar threesome of Cristopher Sanchez, Jesus Luzardo and Zack Wheeler. Those three will be back, with Wheeler in the final year of his deal. That probably indicates one more run with this group. President of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski hasn't held his end-of-season news conference yet, so we don't know exactly what the Phillies have in mind; they did rehire Don Mattingly as manager after Alex Cora reportedly turned them down a second time. They'll address the bullpen and will once again be on the prowl for a right fielder, but the 2027 Phillies will look a lot like the 2026 Phillies.

The New York Yankees will look vastly different when we see them next

Verdict: Not real

Speaking of makeovers, after another early playoff exit, it feels like the Yankees need one. The playoffs ended with a humiliating three-game sweep against the Rays, including an embarrassing four-error game along the way. Much of the criticism that followed focused on the defense, and understandably so -- but it was the offense that once again let down the Yankees. In the Aaron Judge era going back to 2017, the Yankees have hit .225/.310/.396 in the playoffs, with several series-losing flameouts at the plate. Against the Rays, they hit .130 and scored five runs. They could have had Ozzie Smith, Brooks Robinson, Willie Mays and Roberto Clemente playing defense and it wouldn't have mattered.

It has been 17 seasons since their last championship, with only one World Series appearance in 2024. It feels like general manager Brian Cashman needs to do something different ... right?

Yes, but -- like the Phillies -- the Yankees are kind of locked in to their roster. They do have some free agents: You can probably say goodbye to free agents Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trent Grisham and Paul Goldschmidt, although Chisholm expressed a desire to return. Closer David Bednar and top righty setup man Paul Blackburn are free agents, two guys the Yankees will want to re-sign.

But the Yankees are already committed to $202 million in 2027 salaries for just six players: Aaron Judge, Cody Bellinger, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon and Giancarlo Stanton (mercifully, finally in the last year of his deal). Throw in another $16 million for Ryan McMahon. There just isn't a lot of flexibility here for a big makeover. George Lombard and Spencer Jones, the 2026 rookies who will get a full season in 2027, won't change the complexion of the Yankees' offense either. Jones in particular has major strikeout issues.

The rotation will make the Yankees contenders. Relying on what will be a 35-year-old Aaron Judge to carry the offense will only get more precarious as he gets older. They will hit a lot of home runs, as always. But the 2027 Yankees will look a lot like the 2026 Yankees.

stories.headline: What NBA preseason has revealed about the Lakers, 76ers, Celtics and every team
stories.summary: With 2026-27 tipoff closing in, Ben Golliver shares the key takeaways that will shape the regular season.
stories.body:
The NBA preseason is a time to welcome new faces, sort through lineup questions, hype up prospects, squabble over unresolved contract situations and panic about unfortunate injuries before the real competition begins.

With Tuesday's openers fast approaching, let's bounce around the league one final time in search of key takeaways that will shape the upcoming season.

Jump to a team:

ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE

DAL | DEN | DET | GS | HOU | IND

LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN

NO | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX

POR | SAC | SA | TOR | UTAH | WAS

Atlanta Hawks
The preseason revealed ... the backcourt is loaded

With Trae Young's salary no longer on the books, the Hawks have assembled a backcourt rotation stacked with creators Nickeil Alexander-Walker and CJ McCollum, stoppers Dyson Daniels and Lu Dort, shooter Corey Kispert and 2026 lottery pick Kingston Flemings. In fact, Atlanta had such a surplus that it traded two backup guards to land 3-and-D forward Dorian Finney-Smith from the Charlotte Hornets in September.

Hawks coach Quin Snyder has used multiple starting lineups during the preseason, but he's best served sticking with last season's top group -- Alexander-Walker, McCollum, Daniels, Jalen Johnson and Onyeka Okongwu -- because it posted a phenomenal plus-20.3 net rating. That would move Dort to a reserve role after he spent the past six seasons as a starter for the Oklahoma City Thunder.

Boston Celtics
The preseason revealed ... Jayson Tatum will hit the ground running

While Tatum returned from a May 2025 Achilles tear in less than 10 months, his shot looked rusty and he played below his All-NBA standard down the stretch last season. Then, his speedy comeback ended with a whimper when he sat out a Game 7 loss to the Philadelphia 76ers in the first round due to left knee discomfort.

By taking those lumps last season, Tatum prepared himself for a smoother launch in 2026-27. The five-time All-Star was spectacular at times while posting 23 points in 27 minutes during his preseason debut, and his outside shot looked confident in a variety of situations. The Celtics must learn to live without Jaylen Brown and incorporate two key new pieces in forward Paul George and center Mitchell Robinson, but everything will be easier if Tatum is back to performing like an MVP contender.

Brooklyn Nets
The preseason revealed ... Egor Demin is one to watch

Be sure to include Demin on the list of 2025 first-round picks poised for major improvement in their second campaigns. While draft classmates in Dallas' Cooper Flagg and San Antonio's Dylan Harper are bursting with star potential, Demin's goal will be to move past a shaky rookie season and establish himself as a quality starting point guard.

After being content to settle for outside shots as a rookie, the 20-year-old Russian was more forceful off the dribble at Las Vegas summer league. That shift was evident in a preseason win over the 76ers: Midway through the first quarter, Demin drove past LeBron James and finished a difficult layup over Joel Embiid. Veteran forwards Michael Porter Jr. and Julius Randle will handle the bulk of the scoring for Brooklyn, but Demin is arguably the Nets' most important player given his ability to shape their rebuilding effort.

Charlotte Hornets

The preseason revealed ... life without Kon Knueppel is no fun

While Knueppel's record 3-point shooting got all the attention during his rookie season, his reliability was just as important to Charlotte's success. Knueppel averaged 18.5 points per game in 81 appearances, joining Young and Karl-Anthony Towns as the only rookies to hit those scoring and availability marks over the past decade. And despite Knueppel's youth and starter responsibilities, the 2025 No. 4 pick posted a strong plus-6.2 net rating.

Unfortunately, Knueppel has been sidelined throughout the preseason with a hamstring injury and his availability for opening night remains uncertain. Knueppel is a critical player for the retooling Hornets, who pivoted by trading star guard LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves this summer. Charlotte's offense won't sing at full volume until its most prolific shooter is back to 100%.

Chicago Bulls

The preseason revealed ... Caleb Wilson will stop you in your tracks

There's a special joy in watching Wilson explore the bounds of his developing game. Already in his first preseason, the 2026 No. 4 pick has raced out in transition for thunderous dunks, worked through traffic for turnaround midrange jumpers and created space in isolation to launch step-back 3-pointers. That range of offensive skills is rare for a 6-foot-10 rookie forward.

Wilson has a path to becoming the best player in a strong class if he solidifies his outside shooting and smooths out his ballhandling and decision-making. His confidence out of the gate is a positive indicator, and he appears destined to be an impact defender given his length and leaping ability. The Bulls face no immediate pressure to win after changing their general manager and coach, so this season will be all about gawking at Wilson's latest highlights and daydreaming about his potential.

Cleveland Cavaliers
The preseason revealed ... Peyton Watson isn't the only notable newcomer

Get this: The Cavaliers will pay their projected starters more than $179 million in 2026-27, well above this year's $165 million salary cap. Given that top-heavy spending structure, Cleveland will welcome any and all second-unit help.

While Watson was the Cavaliers' biggest offseason addition and plugs in as a starting forward, Mario Hezonja also arrived this summer as a bargain signing after spending the past six seasons in Europe. The 31-year-old Hezonja, who once upon a time was a 2015 lottery pick, averaged 17.5 points per game for Real Madrid in Spain's ACB league last season. His primary task will be to boost Cleveland's bench scoring, which ranked 25th in 2025-26, with his inside-outside versatility.

Dallas Mavericks

The preseason revealed ... the Cooper Flagg hype train is gaining speed

ESPN's Brian Windhorst ably documented Flagg's eye-opening performances during the Mavericks and Rockets' exhibitions at the NBA China Games. While it would be foolish to read too much into preseason statistics, Flagg averaged 25.8 points, 7.8 rebounds, 7.8 assists plus more than a steal and a block per 36 minutes in the two games. Only one player in NBA history has maintained those per-game averages for a full regular season: LeBron James.

The No. 1 pick in the 2025 draft should factor heavily into this year's All-Star conversation, and there's a good chance Flagg will outperform his No. 23 spot in ESPN's NBA Rank if he continues to impact games on both ends like he did in Macao. Flagg's 3-point shot -- he hit under 30% as a rookie -- can still improve, but his combination of instincts, athleticism and work ethic is rare. And remember: He's still a teenager.

Denver Nuggets

The preseason revealed ... Nikola Jokic's passing is getting more preposterous

Jokic delivered the best highlight of the preseason when he casually flipped a no-look, behind-the-back pass from the left baseline past three Utah Jazz defenders to find Cameron Johnson for a right-corner 3. The assist was so on the money that Johnson seemingly didn't move his hands an inch to haul it in, and the crowd was already roaring before the shot went up.

The play was a good reminder that the three-time MVP is entering rarified air as a passer. Jokic led the NBA in assists per game for the first time last season, and the 31-year-old ranks first among centers in career assists. Though Jokic enters the season ranking 41st on the NBA's all-time assist leaderboard, he's only about five seasons away from reaching the top 10 at his recent pace. Somehow, a Serbian center who wasn't selected until the second round of the 2014 draft has a legitimate chance of surpassing all-time great point guards such as Oscar Robertson and Magic Johnson.

Detroit Pistons
The preseason revealed ... cooler heads prevailed in the Jalen Duren saga

While the negotiations weren't pretty and dragged past media day, Detroit avoided all the nightmare scenarios by finally inking the All-Star center to a five-year, $200 million contract extension on Oct. 1. The Pistons didn't fork over anything close to max money, they don't need to worry about Duren playing half-heartedly on a qualifying offer, and he can't walk next summer as an unrestricted free agent. Detroit's core of Cade Cunningham, Duren and Ausar Thompson is officially locked in for years to come.

Duren took a major step to move past the ordeal by stating that he's a "Detroit Piston for life" during a conciliatory news conference. Now, the focus shifts back to the court, where expectations will be sky-high following the Pistons' 60-win campaign in 2025-26. Duren's role shouldn't change dramatically, though his defensive impact could come under greater scrutiny after Detroit traded backup center Isaiah Stewart to the Memphis Grizzlies in June.

Golden State Warriors

The preseason revealed ... Podz got paid

The Warriors' pile of questions got only bigger during the preseason due to Kristaps Porzingis' mysterious indefinite absence just months after Golden State signed him to a two-year, $40 million contract. Warriors coach Steve Kerr is already trying to get by without injured star Jimmy Butler III, and Porzingis' availability concerns feel like a blow this roster can't sustain.

In brighter news, 23-year-old guard Brandin Podziemski signed a five-year, $110 million rookie extension earlier this month. While the confident scorer is less accomplished than most of the other players from the 2023 draft who inked extensions this cycle, his signing reflects Golden State's need to prepare for the future with Stephen Curry, Butler, Draymond Green and Al Horford all approaching the twilight of their careers. Podziemski's $22 million AAV puts him in the same ballpark as fellow guards Christian Braun, Malik Monk and CJ McCollum. Within that group last season, Podziemski ranked first in win shares and second in scoring.

Houston Rockets

The preseason revealed ... Fred VanVleet is back with a bang

The Rockets took a lot of heat when their offense fell flat in last season's playoffs due to spacing and playmaking concerns. In his preseason debut, VanVleet wasted no time reminding observers that he remains Houston's best solution. After missing last season with a knee injury, VanVleet posted 17 points and seven assists to key a convincing exhibition win over the Mavericks in his first game action in nearly 18 months.

The 32-year-old point guard launched 12 3-pointers, twice as many as Houston's other starters combined. VanVleet's return should produce some trickle-down benefits: Kevin Durant and Alperen Sengun will have another trustworthy ball handler for late-clock and late-game situations, and Reed Sheppard should enjoy cleaner looks when he plays alongside the veteran floor general.

Indiana Pacers

The preseason revealed ... Tyrese Haliburton can still tug on the heartstrings

Haliburton's Achilles tear during Game 7 of the 2025 Finals was one of the most heartbreaking and consequential in-game injuries in NBA history. The underdog Pacers were knocking on the doorstep of their first championship after a series of miracle playoff comebacks, only for their All-Star guard to go down with an injury that also cost him the entire 2025-26 season.

Fast-forward to last week: Haliburton made his preseason debut against the Minnesota Timberwolves at Iowa State, his alma mater. The former Cyclones star purchased thousands of tickets to fill the student sections and thanked the crowd before scoring seven points and dishing six assists in limited minutes. "It's been 472 days since I've played a game of basketball," he said. "I wouldn't want to do it anywhere else except my second home." The heartwarming scene in Ames was the perfect way for Haliburton to complete his grueling injury rehabilitation and get back to work.

LA Clippers

The preseason revealed ... Darius Garland had better have a career year

The Clippers' injury news went from bad to worse when guard Max Strus suffered a right foot injury just five minutes into the first quarter of their preseason opener. Strus, who is expected to miss at least a month, joins teammates Brandon Ingram, Jordan Miller and Yanic Konan Niederhauser with long-term injuries. Meanwhile, Bradley Beal has been sidelined this preseason with right knee inflammation.

To make matters worse, five of the Clippers' top six scorers from last season are no longer on the team, leaving Garland, a two-time All-Star point guard, as the last man standing. A passable offense will hinge on Garland shifting to a score-first mindset to compensate for the lack of firepower around him. While Rui Hachimura and rookie Keaton Wagler should also enjoy green lights, LA's offense will likely be a grind until Ingram returns.

Los Angeles Lakers
The preseason revealed ... surprisingly, title talk is in the air

The Lakers are brimming with optimism after a transformative offseason, during which LeBron James departed and a new cast of role players arrived in Hollywood. Luka Doncic and coach JJ Redick have both floated championship aspirations, even though the Lakers were swept out of the conference semifinals last season and underwent an out-of-nowhere ownership change in August. Another potentially major hang-up: The Lakers entered training camp with two unclaimed spots in their starting lineup.

While Doncic and guard Austin Reaves have an excellent bond, the Lakers clearly trail behind most of the leading title favorites when it comes to continuity. But from a talent and fit perspective, the Lakers can claim some resemblance to the 2023-24 Mavericks now that center Walker Kessler is in place. Doncic led that Dallas team to 50 wins and a surprise trip to the Finals.

Memphis Grizzlies

The preseason revealed ... Zach Edey is still a force

With Ja Morant, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Desmond Bane all departing the Grizzlies in separate trades since June 2025, it's easy to forget that Memphis has welcomed back a major talent as it ramps up for a rebuilding campaign. Edey, a 7-foot-3 center who played only 11 games last season before undergoing season-ending ankle surgery, has returned to claim his spot as the Grizzlies' starting center. In Friday's exhibition win over the Bulls, Edey made his presence felt with 10 points and five rebounds in just 16 minutes.

The 2024 lottery pick has the size and strength to control the glass and punish small-ball lineups in the paint, but Memphis must use this season to craft a sustainable role for him given his immense frame and history of lower-body injuries. Despite its roster overhaul, Memphis has assembled a solid frontcourt rotation that also includes Rookie of the Year contender Cameron Boozer and bruising backup center Isaiah Stewart. If Edey can put his injury woes behind him -- a big if -- the Grizzlies should be competing for a spot in the play-in tournament before too long.

Miami Heat

The preseason revealed ... Giannis Antetokounmpo made a good first impression

It will take months to get used to seeing Antetokounmpo in a Heat jersey after his 13-year run with the Milwaukee Bucks, but so far No. 7 in white has looked a lot like No. 34 in green on the court. Antetokounmpo pummeled the New Orleans Pelicans in a recent exhibition, blasting through a crowded paint for punishing dunks, racing ahead in transition to aid Miami's preferred up-tempo approach and making the proper reads after drawing multiple defenders.

Given how much time Antetokounmpo missed due to injuries last season and the career-altering trade that shaped his summer, the two-time MVP is off to a promising start with the Heat. Offseason concerns about Miami's 3-point shooting acumen haven't really materialized in the preseason, though it's fair to question whether the Heat have enough talent beyond Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo to keep pace with the East's best.

Milwaukee Bucks

The preseason revealed ... the veterans will get first dibs

Many teams mix and match their starting lineups during the preseason to test various configurations or rest veterans, but new Bucks coach Taylor Jenkins has made sure his most accomplished players have been on the floor together. That makes sense: It will take time for the post-Antetokounmpo Bucks to mesh their holdover pieces with a batch of former Heat players who arrived in this summer's blockbuster.

Milwaukee appears ready to enter the season with Ryan Rollins, Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kyle Kuzma and Myles Turner as its starting five, a group that will likely struggle to reach league average on offense and defense. As the season unfolds, Jenkins must decide when to prioritize the development of younger players such as Kel'el Ware and 2026 lottery picks Brayden Burries and Nate Ament. While that possible shift could be aided by unloading players at the trade deadline, the balance of present and future won't be influenced by draft positioning -- the Bucks have already traded away their 2027 first-round pick.

Minnesota Timberwolves

The preseason revealed ... the vibes are looser

Timberwolves coach Chris Finch recently summarized his team's new identity in succinct fashion: "We've traded moodiness for giddiness." That checks out, given that Minnesota spent the summer pairing Anthony Edwards with LaMelo Ball in a charismatic Zoomer backcourt and moving on from Julius Randle and Naz Reid. Throw in forward Jonathan Kuminga, who was signed in free agency, and the Timberwolves have seemingly transformed from "Edwards and a bunch of veterans" to "Rudy Gobert and a bunch of young guys."

But Finch surely understands that Minnesota faces serious competition in the West's playoff bracket. The initial giddiness that comes with any honeymoon period must eventually be complemented by resolve and maturity. The Timberwolves' offense should be more fun and less predictable with Ball in the mix, but discipline and focus in high-pressure moments loom as hurdles.

New Orleans Pelicans

The preseason revealed ... the prospects are taking a back seat

The Pelicans' roster-building strategy has been puzzling. After winning just 26 games last season, are they trying to squeeze better results from a mediocre roster or are they ready to start building the future? Jamahl Mosley, hired as coach in May, appears to be leaning toward competitiveness rather than development.

Mosley opened the preseason with a veteran-dominated starting lineup featuring Zion Williamson, Dejounte Murray, Trey Murphy III, Herbert Jones and Yves Missi. In turn, 2025 lottery picks Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen both came off the bench. While Fears, 19, and Queen, 21, combined for 97 starts last season, both struggled to score efficiently as rookies and now must start over with their second coach in two seasons. The Pelicans are a team to watch in the run-up to the trade deadline: If the wins don't materialize in a meaningful way, the right move would be to hand over more responsibilities to the youngsters.

New York Knicks

The preseason revealed ... James Dolan isn't afraid to be the villain

The NBA's parity era has been brutal on defending champions. Each of the past eight have lost key players, encountered untimely injuries, or simply run out of gas in attempts to defend their titles. The pace of modern basketball makes it nearly impossible for teams to hold up for 100-plus games in consecutive seasons, and the current collective bargaining agreement's onerous apron penalties are always lurking, ready to break up juggernauts.

Knicks owner James Dolan has taken an unsentimental approach to those harsh realities: His desire to avoid the second apron led to backup center Mitchell Robinson's offseason departure, and the Knicks' recent statement that they have paused negotiation talks with Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart wasn't exactly welcome news. "Very disappointed to say the least," Towns said this week. If New York follows recent precedent and falters in its title defense, Dolan has set himself up to be viewed as the billionaire bogeyman who let money ruin his organization's rare moment in the sun.

Oklahoma City Thunder
The preseason revealed ... Aday Mara is found gold

Mara struggled to make a positive impact when surrounded by fringe talent in the unstructured confines of the Las Vegas summer league, but the enormous Spanish center has hit the ground running with the loaded Thunder in the preseason. It already feels unfair that Oklahoma City landed him with the 12th pick in June's draft: During a standout exhibition against the Bucks, Mara finished lobs, tossed backdoor passes, left Kel'el Ware grasping at air with spin moves in the post and made all 10 of his field goal attempts. For fans of a certain generation who prize deft footwork from big men, Mara is a gift that will keep on giving all season.

The Thunder clearly concluded they needed more interior size after their Western Conference finals loss to Victor Wembanyama's San Antonio Spurs, and the 7-foot-2 Mara will make it easier for coach Mark Daigneault to manage the 82-game slog. There should be minutes available because starting center Isaiah Hartenstein has missed 37% of Oklahoma City's games over the past two seasons, and Mara has enough offensive skill and versatility to function alongside any of the Thunder's other big men.

Orlando Magic

The preseason revealed ... Tristan da Silva is launching

It's always worth monitoring which role players benefit or suffer when a new coach arrives. In Orlando, da Silva has been reaping the rewards of first-time head coach Sean Sweeney's emphasis on spacing and ball movement. Though da Silva averaged a modest 3.7 3-point attempts during his first two seasons with the Magic, the 2024 first-round pick launched 10.7 treys per game in his first three preseason appearances.

For context, only Stephen Curry, Luka Doncic and LaMelo Ball attempted more than 10 per game last season, and no player in Magic history has averaged more than 7.7. Empowering da Silva makes sense for Sweeney given that Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner are inconsistent outside shooters; Orlando's star forwards should theoretically become more efficient offensive weapons with more room inside the arc.

Philadelphia 76ers

The preseason revealed ... LeBron James' latest superteam is pacing itself

The veteran-laden 76ers haven't exactly raced out of the gate: In Philadelphia's first three exhibition games, James took a total of one shot and logged only 18 minutes while coach Nick Nurse rotated 10 players into his starting lineups. Given James' age (41) and Joel Embiid's injury history (extensive), the Sixers are obviously more focused on April, May and June than October and November.

Don't be surprised if Philadelphia's slow feel-out period continues into the regular season. James has a history of rough beginnings when he changes teams: The 2010-11 Heat started 9-8, the 2014-15 Cavaliers started 5-7 and the 2018-19 Lakers started 4-6. Of course, Miami and Cleveland went on to reach the NBA Finals, so it's probably best to reserve judgment on the 76ers until at least Thanksgiving.

Phoenix Suns
The preseason revealed ... Khaman Maluach is coming along

The Suns project as a low-ceiling team that won't generate much excitement beyond Arizona's borders: Devin Booker and Jalen Green form a fine backcourt pairing, but they don't exactly put a scare into the elite teams in the West. If Phoenix can escape the play-in tournament as it did in 2025-26, that will qualify as a successful season. The exception to its ho-hum vibe is Maluach, a 20-year-old center who barely played as a rookie last season.

The 7-foot-1 Maluach was bigger, stronger and better than the Las Vegas summer league competition in July, and he built on that showing with a well-rounded performance against Victor Wembanyama's Spurs on Saturday. Maluach is more than just a dunker and a shot blocker: Against San Antonio, he fed a cutter from the high post, stepped out to hit a 3-pointer and came up with a steal while trapping outside the arc. The Suns should be able to give their 2025 lottery pick plenty of developmental minutes as they wait for starting center Mark Williams to return from September shoulder surgery.

Portland Trail Blazers

The preseason revealed ... Ja Morant should come off the bench

Damian Lillard's early returns represent some good news for the Blazers, who endured a brutal summer marked by stalled arena negotiations and a botched broadcasting hire. Despite sitting out last season because of an Achilles injury, the 36-year-old star has generally looked sharp and shot the ball well in exhibition action. Though Portland should still be careful with his early-season ramp-up, Lillard's readiness brings much-needed clarity to a guard-heavy roster.

The best way for new coach Micah Nori to balance his lineups is to play Lillard alongside Scoot Henderson or Jrue Holiday then move Morant -- a surprising summer trade acquisition -- to the bench. Morant has been less impressive in the preseason, and Nori should not feel obligated to defer to his star power. Shifting Morant to the second unit also would benefit Deni Avdija, who should be treated as the centerpiece of this refashioned roster.

Sacramento Kings
The preseason revealed ... Maxime Raynaud dodged a bullet

Though not exactly a household name, the 2025 second-round pick was a bright spot during the Kings' miserable 2025-26 season. Raynaud averaged 12.5 points and 7.5 rebounds to earn second-team All-Rookie honors, establishing himself as a rare hit for an organization with a checkered draft history.

The Kings appear headed for another dismal season after losing their first four exhibition games, but they caught a break when Raynaud apparently avoided a serious right knee injury in a loss to the Warriors on Saturday. After exiting the court in a wheel chair, the 23-year-old French center was diagnosed with a patellar subluxation that will force him to sit out the season opener but should allow him to return relatively soon. Given Sacramento's roster is short on young talent to grow with 2026 lottery pick Darius Acuff Jr., a more serious injury for Raynaud would have been a crushing blow.

San Antonio Spurs

The preseason revealed ... San Antonio is close to answering to its biggest question

No team is facing a more consequential lineup decision than the Spurs, who must decide whether to make room for 2025 No. 2 pick Dylan Harper in a starting lineup that has included guards De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle and Devin Vassell. Though San Antonio's decision will shape its internal chemistry, the 2027 title race and Harper's ascent, the reigning Western Conference champions haven't officially tipped their hand. With Fox sitting out the Spurs' first three preseason games, the lineup debate has raged on in his absence.

The Spurs don't have much on-court evidence to go on because Fox, Castle and Harper shared the court for only 25 minutes during the 2025-26 regular season. Victor Wembanyama's singular defensive presence nullifies most of the usual concerns about conceding size with a three- or four-guard lineup, but coach Mitch Johnson does still need a high-level playmaker to lead his second unit. When push comes to shove, San Antonio should bet on Harper's potential, move Vassell to the bench, start Tobias Harris at power forward and give the three-guard lineup an extended test drive. To make that plan work, Johnson must creatively stagger his rotations to ensure that either Fox or Harper is always on the court.

Toronto Raptors
The preseason revealed ... Kawhi Leonard is ready to turn the page

Understandably, Leonard never had much to say about the NBA's yearlong investigation of the Clippers' role in salary cap circumvention. Even after the punishments were doled out and he was officially traded to the Raptors, Leonard sidestepped the issue at a September news conference by saying that he wanted to "move forward and focus on my time being a Toronto Raptor."

The best way for Leonard to actually turn the page is to play at an All-NBA level and lead Toronto to meaningful playoff success. The two-time Finals MVP got off to a great start on that front during his preseason debut Tuesday, torching the undermanned Knicks for 21 points in only 17 minutes. Raptors coach Darko Rajakovic should be thrilled to finally have a certified alpha scorer; no Toronto player has averaged 25 points since Leonard departed for the Clippers in 2019.

Utah Jazz
The preseason revealed ... the offense should be light years better

Utah has a strong case to be the NBA's most improved team from a watchability standpoint. Though that statement says something about how miserable the Jazz's defense was during their 22-win season in 2025-26, it also hints at the significant potential of this season's upgraded offense.

Lauri Markkanen, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Keyonte George are all proven high-level scorers, and 2026 No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson should be at or near the top of his class in points per game. Importantly, the Jazz's whole should be greater than the sum of its parts because their most important players are all effective floor spacers and willing passers. After ranking 22nd in offensive efficiency last season, Utah could jump 10 spots if it gets a Rookie of the Year-worthy season from Peterson plus good health for Markkanen and Jackson.

Washington Wizards
The preseason revealed ... Trae Young's pass-first pledge looks real

When Young met with reporters in July after signing a four-year, $212 million extension, he made it clear that his primary responsibility was to keep the Wizards' many scoring options involved in the offense. Young suggested he would be taking a more pass-first approach to get the most out of a roster that features 10-time All-Star Anthony Davis, 2026 No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa, 2024 No. 2 pick Alex Sarr, 2025 No. 6 pick Tre Johnson and Kyshawn George, among other capable scorers.

Sure enough, Young dished 23 assists and attempted only 16 shots through Washington's first three preseason games. That's quite the extreme makeover for a four-time All-Star guard who has averaged 18.3 shots during his eight-year career, but radical measures are in order after the Wizards ranked 29th in offensive efficiency and 28th in assist-to-turnover ratio last season.

stories.headline: Transfer rumors, news: Martínez's future at Man United in doubt after bust-up
stories.summary: Lisandro Martínez's future at Manchester United is in question after he pointed fingers at the club's board. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
Lisandro Martínez's future at Manchester United is in question after his scathing critique of the club's board, while Bayern Munich could offer Florian Wirtz an escape route from the Premier League should he want to end his stay at Liverpool.

Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.
